title: Our senses: many more than five
playtest: Checked every hands-on part as if done at home today. Hold Your Nose: sugar with a pinch of ground elaichi, dalchini or saunf tastes 'just sweet' with the nose pinched. The spice appears the moment you let go. Lumps of spice can give it away, so mix finely. Two-Point Test: both toothpicks must stick out equally. The steps now say a grown-up pokes the holes and checks each tester on a palm first. The forearm and back often feel 4 cm as one point, and the example chart shows that. Point at the Sound: a hand over the ear blocks only part of the sound. So a cotton-wool tip was added, with softer clicks to try if both scores come out the same. Feel the Sound: the cling-film drum only works if the film is tight and the plate is banged close. The steps now give the distance, one hand's length, and use light sugar grains. A phone bass note is the back-up. Blue Mango: a blue mango with a pink leaf gives a clear yellow mango with a green leaf. It needs thick colouring, good light and a full 30 seconds of staring. Fading Coin: some children never lose the coin, and the note says that is normal. Train Your Nose: day 1 scores of 2 or 3 out of 6 are normal. Testing a family member who did not practise helps rule out luck. Super-Sense Pairs works alone, by counting turns. Kim's Game needs a second person to set up each round. Everything uses things found in most Indian kitchens. Check for food allergies before any tasting. Never sniff spices hard, and never put anything inside the ear canal. Senses You Forgot You Had: standing on one foot is much harder with the eyes shut for almost every child, so the steps put a wall and a grown-up close by. The three-bowl test works when the warm and cold bowls are clearly different from the middle one. A grown-up checks the warm bowl with an elbow first, so it is never hot.

summary.text: Pinch your nose, and a spoon of elaichi sugar tastes only sweet. Let go, and the elaichi comes back, because most of what we call taste is really smell. A sense is a way your body detects something and tells the brain. People often say we have five senses, but that list comes from the Greek thinker Aristotle, more than 2,300 years ago. Scientists count many more: balance, knowing where your body parts are, warmth and cold, pain, thirst, and sensors inside you that check your blood. In every sense, special cells called receptors turn what they detect into tiny electric signals, and nerves carry the signals to the brain. Other animals detect things we cannot, like ultraviolet light or echoes in the dark. Nobody yet knows how electric signals in a brain become the taste of a mango.
summary.art: A child in the middle of a kitchen with many glowing paths running into her ear, fingertip, tongue, nose, eye, inner ear and tummy, all turning into the same little sparks as they reach her head.

intro.hook: Shut your eyes and pinch your nose. Now someone puts a pinch of sugar on your tongue. It has a secret spice mixed in. Can you tell which spice it is? Keep pinching. Now let go of your nose.
intro.text: When you let go, the spice suddenly appears. Your tongue did not change. Your nose started working again. Next, you follow each sense from the outside of your body down to tiny cells and electric signals. You also find out that you have many more than five senses. And you find out what a bat, a fly and a snake can sense that you cannot.
intro.art: A child with eyes shut, pinching her nose with one hand and holding a spoon of sugar with the other, a little cloud of cardamom smell waiting outside her nostrils.

outcomes: I can say what a sense is: a way the body detects something from the world and sends a message to the brain.
I can explain how hearing works, from shaking air to the eardrum, three tiny bones, hair cells in the cochlea and the brain. I can show why two ears help find where a sound comes from.
I can explain that skin has different receptors for different kinds of touch, and show with a fair test where touch is sharpest.
I can name the five basic tastes, explain that the tongue map is wrong, and say why chilli is not a taste.
I can explain that flavour is mostly smell, and show it with a test where I pinch my nose.
I can explain that eyes detect light with rods and cones, and that every sense turns the world into the same kind of electric signal.
I can give examples of animals that sense things humans cannot, and say what scientists still do not know about how senses become experience.
I can explain that we have many more than five senses, such as balance, body position, warmth and cold, and thirst, and test some of them at home.

terms.meaning: A way your body finds out about the world. It detects something, like light or sound, and sends a message to your brain. To detect something means to notice that it is there.
terms.example: Hearing is a sense. It tells you a pressure cooker is whistling, even when you are in another room.
terms.art: A pressure cooker whistling in a kitchen, and a child in the next room turning her head towards the sound.

terms.meaning: A part of the body built to detect one kind of thing. Ears, eyes, nose, tongue and skin are the best-known sense organs. The balance organs deep inside your ears are sense organs too.
terms.example: Your nose is the sense organ for smell.
terms.art: A friendly row of sense organs: an ear, an eye, a nose, a tongue, a hand, and the curled balance tubes of the inner ear.

terms.meaning: The sense that tells you which way is down and when your head tilts or turns. Its receptors are hair cells in the inner ear, next to the cochlea. Scientists call it the vestibular sense.
terms.example: Spin round and stop. The room seems to keep spinning, because the liquid in your balance organs is still moving.
terms.art: A child standing on one foot with arms out, and a cut-away of the inner ear showing three curved tubes beside the snail-shaped cochlea.

terms.meaning: The sense of where the parts of your body are and how they are moving. Stretch sensors in your muscles and joints send the signals. Say it pro-pree-oh-SEP-shun.
terms.example: With your eyes shut, you can still touch your nose with one finger.
terms.art: A child with eyes closed touching the tip of her nose with one finger, with little glowing dots in her arm muscles.

terms.meaning: Sensing what is happening inside your own body. Sensors inside you notice a full bladder, a stretched stomach, thirst and the carbon dioxide in your blood.
terms.example: Thirst is interoception. Cells in your brain notice when your blood gets too salty, and you want a drink.
terms.art: A child holding a glass of water, with a simple outline of her body showing small glowing sensors in the brain, stomach and bladder.

terms.meaning: A special cell that notices one kind of thing, like light, a push or a chemical. When it notices it, it makes a tiny electric signal.
terms.example: Your eyes have receptors that notice light. Your tongue has receptors that notice sugar.
terms.art: A single round cell with a little antenna, sparking when a speck of light touches it.

terms.meaning: The tiny living building block that bodies are made of. Your body has many millions of millions of cells, of many different kinds.
terms.example: Skin cells, blood cells and nerve cells are all cells.
terms.art: A zoom from a fingertip down to a patch of tiny cells, like bricks in a wall.

terms.meaning: A long thread made of nerve cells that carries messages between your body and your brain.
terms.example: When you touch a hot tawa, nerves carry the message from your finger to your brain in a tiny fraction of a second.
terms.art: A hand with a glowing thread running from the fingertip up the arm to the head.

terms.meaning: A tiny pulse of electricity that travels along a nerve. Every sense sends its messages to the brain as nerve signals.
terms.example: The fastest nerve signals travel about 100 metres in one second. That is the length of a football field.
terms.art: A line of little sparks racing along a nerve thread, with a stopwatch beside it.

terms.meaning: The part inside your head that receives the nerve signals from all your senses and puts them together into one world.
terms.example: Your brain puts the sight, the sound and the smell of a frying pakora together, so you know what it is at once.
terms.art: A brain inside a head, with lines coming in from the eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin and joining in the middle.

terms.meaning: Fast shaking, backwards and forwards. Sound is a vibration that travels through air, water or solid things.
terms.example: Touch your throat while you hum. You can feel it vibrate.
terms.art: A child's fingers on her throat while she hums, with little wavy lines around them.

terms.meaning: A thin, tight skin at the inner end of your ear canal. It shakes when sound reaches it, like the skin of a tabla.
terms.example: When someone claps, the shaking air makes your eardrum shake too.
terms.art: A cut-away ear showing the ear canal and a thin round eardrum at the end, like a tiny drum.

terms.meaning: A small tube coiled like a snail shell, deep inside your ear. It is full of liquid and lined with hair cells.
terms.example: The cochlea is about the size of a pea.
terms.art: A snail-shaped coil next to a green pea, the same size.

terms.meaning: A receptor in the cochlea with a tiny tuft on top. When sound shakes the liquid, the tuft bends and the cell makes a nerve signal.
terms.example: Each ear has about 15,000 hair cells. Very loud sounds can break them, and they do not grow back.
terms.art: A row of cells with little tufts on top, bending like grass in the wind.

terms.meaning: A tiny bunch of taste receptor cells, shaped like a flower bud. Most are in the little bumps on your tongue.
terms.example: You have a few thousand taste buds. Each one has dozens of taste cells.
terms.art: A magnified bump on a tongue with tiny bud shapes inside it.

terms.meaning: The savoury, meaty basic taste. It is one of the five basic tastes, with sweet, sour, salty and bitter.
terms.example: Ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, cheese and a good sambar have lots of umami.
terms.art: A bowl of steaming sambar beside a cut ripe tomato and some mushrooms.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece of a substance that is still that substance. It is far too small to see, and it is made of atoms joined together. Smells and tastes come from molecules.
terms.example: When you open a jar of elaichi, some of its molecules float out into the air and up your nose.
terms.art: An open jar of cardamom pods with tiny coloured balls drifting out of it towards a nose.

terms.meaning: What you notice when you eat. It is taste from the tongue mixed with smell from the nose, plus touch and temperature.
terms.example: With a blocked nose, food tastes flat. You still taste sweet and salty, but the flavour has gone.
terms.art: A child with a cold and a blocked nose, looking sadly at a bowl of her favourite khichdi.

terms.meaning: A thin layer at the back of the eye that detects light. It is covered in two kinds of receptor cells, rods and cones.
terms.example: The picture you see is made on your retina first, upside down.
terms.art: A cut-away eye with light rays entering and an upside-down tree drawn on the back wall.

terms.meaning: The two kinds of light receptor in the retina. Rods work in dim light but see no colour. Cones need more light and see colour.
terms.example: At night in a dark room, you see shapes but hardly any colour. Only your rods are working.
terms.art: Tall thin rod cells and short pointed cone cells side by side, the cones in three colours.

terms.meaning: A ghost picture you see after staring at something bright. It happens because some of the colour cells in your eye, called cones, get tired. Scientists call this tiredness adaptation.
terms.example: Stare at a red square for 30 seconds. Then look at a white wall. You see a green-blue square.
terms.art: A red square on paper and, beside it, a white wall with a faint green-blue square floating on it.

terms.meaning: Finding things by making a sound and listening for its echo, the sound bouncing back.
terms.example: Bats find moths in the dark by echolocation. Some blind people do it too, with tongue clicks.
terms.art: A bat sending out curved sound lines that bounce off a moth and come back.

terms.meaning: A German word scientists use for the world as one kind of animal senses it. Every animal has its own Umwelt.
terms.example: A dog's Umwelt is full of smells. A bat's Umwelt is full of echoes.
terms.art: The same garden drawn three ways: as a dog smells it in clouds, as a bee sees it with ultraviolet patterns, and as a person sees it.

terms.meaning: What your brain makes out of the signals from your senses. It is the world as you experience it.
terms.example: Your eyes send signals. Your perception is 'a yellow mango on the table'.
terms.art: Eye signals as little sparks going into a head, and a thought bubble showing a yellow mango.

explanations.definition: A sense is a way the body detects something from the world, or from inside itself, and turns it into a message for the brain. Each sense has its own receptors.
explanations.description: Every sense works in three steps. First, something from the world reaches the body. It might be light, shaking air, a push on the skin or a chemical. Second, receptors detect it. A receptor is a special cell that detects one kind of thing. When it detects it, it makes a tiny electric signal. Third, nerves carry the signal to the brain. Only then do you see, hear, feel, taste or smell. People often say we have five senses: sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell. That list comes from the Greek thinker Aristotle, more than 2,300 years ago. It is a tradition, not a scientific count. Scientists count many more. This unit starts with the five well-known senses, then meets the others.
examples: Hearing: shaking air reaches your ear, hair cells detect it, and a nerve carries the signal to your brain.
Smell: molecules of hot jalebi float up your nose, smell receptors detect them, and your brain says 'jalebi'.
Touch: a mosquito lands on your arm, touch receptors in your skin detect the tiny push, and you swat it.
explanations.art: Three simple steps drawn as a comic strip: a bell ringing, an ear catching the sound, and a spark travelling up a nerve to the brain.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a sense is, and the three steps every sense follows.

explanations.definition: The body has far more than five senses. Besides sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell, it senses balance, the position of its parts, warmth, cold, pain, and many things inside itself.
explanations.description: The list of five senses comes from Aristotle, who picked one sense for each organ you can see. Many senses have no organ you can point to. Your balance sense is in your inner ear, next to the cochlea. Some of its hair cells sit under a layer of jelly topped with tiny crystals. Gravity tugs on the crystals when you tilt your head. Three curved tubes full of liquid tell you when your head turns. Proprioception comes from stretch sensors in your muscles and joints. It tells you where your arms and legs are, even in the dark. Your skin has separate nerve endings for warmth, for cold and for pain. Inside each tooth, under the hard enamel, nerves feel cold and pressure. There are sensors deep inside you too. Stretch sensors tell you when your stomach is full or your bladder needs emptying. Cells in your brain notice when your blood is too salty, and you feel thirsty. When you hold your breath, the strong need to breathe comes mostly from sensors that notice carbon dioxide building up in your blood. Scientists do not agree on the exact number of senses. Depending on how they count, it is somewhere between about a dozen and over 30.
examples: Stand on one foot and close your eyes. It is much harder, because your brain balances with your eyes, your inner ears and your muscle sensors together.
Put one hand in cold water and one in warm water for a minute. Then put both in the same lukewarm water. One hand feels warm and the other feels cold.
explanations.art: An outline of a child's body with small glowing sensors in the inner ear, the muscles of an arm, a tooth, the skin, the stomach, the bladder and the brain, each with a tiny label icon.
explanations.context: People often say we have five senses. This card shows the many other senses your body has, and how you can feel some of them at home.

explanations.concept: Every sense speaks the same language: electric signals
explanations.definition: Every sense turns what it detects into the same kind of message: tiny pulses of electricity called nerve signals. The brain never receives light, sound or smell itself. It only receives signals.
explanations.description: Light never reaches your brain. Sound never reaches it either. What reaches it are tiny electric pulses, travelling along nerves. A signal from your eye looks almost exactly like a signal from your ear. So how does the brain know which is which? It goes by where the signal arrives. Signals from the eyes go to the seeing parts of the brain. Signals from the ears go to the hearing parts. In the 1830s, a German scientist called Johannes Müller pointed out a clue. If the eye or its nerve is pressed, a person sees flashes of light, even in the dark. The nerve from the eye can only send one message: 'light'. That is why rubbing your closed eyes can make you see sparkles. Do not press on your eyes to try it.
examples: When people bump the back of their head hard, they may 'see stars'. The seeing part of the brain is at the back of the head. The bump sets off signals there, so they see light that is not there.
A signal from your tongue saying 'sweet' and a signal from your skin saying 'cold' are both little electric pulses. Only their path is different.
explanations.art: Five different things, a light ray, a sound wave, a smell cloud, a sugar crystal and a pressing finger, each entering a sense organ and all coming out the other side as identical little sparks on their way to the brain.
explanations.context: Your senses detect very different things: light, sound, smells. This card explains the surprise that they all send the brain the same kind of message.

explanations.definition: Sound is a vibration of the air. The ear passes the vibration inwards to hair cells in the cochlea, and the hair cells turn it into nerve signals.
explanations.description: When a bell rings, it shakes the air around it. The shaking travels through the air to you. Your ear flap collects it and funnels it down the ear canal. At the end is the eardrum, a thin tight skin like the top of a tabla. The eardrum shakes. Behind it are the three smallest bones in your body, called the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. The stirrup is about as big as a grain of rice. The three bones pass the shaking on to the cochlea, a liquid-filled tube coiled like a snail shell. The liquid ripples. Inside are about 15,000 hair cells, each with a tiny tuft on top. When the tufts bend, tiny gates in the cell open, and the cell makes a nerve signal. High sounds bend hair cells near the start of the coil. Low sounds bend hair cells near the far end. So the cochlea is laid out a little like the keys of a harmonium. A Hungarian scientist, Georg von Békésy, worked this out, and won a Nobel Prize for it in 1961.
examples: Hum with your fingers on your throat. You feel the vibration that will travel through the air to someone's ear.
Children can hear very high squeaks that most grown-ups cannot, because hair cells for the highest sounds wear out first as we get older.
explanations.art: A cut-away ear in five labelled steps: ear flap, ear canal, eardrum, three tiny bones, and the snail-shaped cochlea with a close-up of bending hair cells.
explanations.context: How does the sound of a temple bell get from the bell into your brain? This card follows it all the way, step by step.

explanations.concept: Two ears find where a sound comes from
explanations.definition: The brain finds where a sound comes from by comparing the two ears. A sound from one side reaches the nearer ear a tiny bit sooner and a little louder.
explanations.description: Think of a sound on your left. It reaches your left ear first. It has to travel around your head to reach your right ear. The difference is less than one thousandth of a second. Your brain notices even that. The right ear also hears the sound a little more quietly, because your head is in the way. Your brain compares both clues and points you towards the sound. A sound straight in front of you or straight behind you reaches both ears at the same moment. So those are the hardest to place. The folds of your ear flap help with that. They change the sound slightly depending on where it comes from, so your brain can tell front from back.
examples: A barn owl's ears are at different heights on its head. So it can tell up from down as well as left from right, and catch a mouse in total darkness.
When you are not sure where a sound is, you turn your head. That gives your brain new clues to compare.
explanations.art: A top view of a child's head with a ringing phone on the left, and two sound paths: a short one to the left ear and a longer one curving round the head to the right ear.
explanations.context: With your eyes shut, you can still point to a sound. This card explains how your two ears work it out together.

explanations.concept: Hair cells that never grow back
explanations.definition: In people, hair cells in the cochlea do not grow back once they are broken. Very loud sounds, or loud sounds for a long time, can break them.
explanations.description: A hair cell's tuft is very delicate. A firecracker going off close by, or loud music in earphones every day, can bend the tufts so hard that they break. Your body cannot make new hair cells to replace them. So hearing lost this way stays lost. Ringing in the ears after a loud noise is a warning sign. Here is a surprise. Birds can grow new hair cells. Scientists found this in the 1980s, and they are still trying to work out how humans might do it too.
examples: A simple rule for earphones: if someone sitting next to you can hear your music, it is too loud.
Cover your ears or move away when firecrackers go off nearby.
explanations.art: Two rows of hair cells: a healthy row standing up like grass, and a damaged row bent and broken after a loud bang.
explanations.context: Your hearing depends on tiny hair cells deep in your ear. This card explains why they need looking after.

explanations.definition: Skin has several kinds of touch receptor. Some detect light touch, some detect steady pressure, some detect vibration and some detect stretching. Other nerve endings detect heat, cold and pain.
explanations.description: Your skin is your biggest sense organ. It is packed with nerve endings. Some of them are wrapped in tiny capsules. Some detect the lightest stroke, like a feather. Some detect steady pressure, like a heavy bag on your lap. Some detect vibration, the fast shaking of a phone on silent mode. Some detect your skin stretching when you bend a finger. When the skin is pushed, the receptor gets squashed a tiny bit. That opens tiny gates in it, and it makes a nerve signal. The gate for touch is made of a protein called Piezo2. An American scientist, Ardem Patapoutian, found it, and won a Nobel Prize in 2021. Fingertips, lips and the tongue have touch receptors packed very close together. Your back has them spread far apart. So fingertips feel much more detail. In one test, people could feel the difference between surfaces whose bumps were only about 13 millionths of a millimetre high.
examples: People who read Braille feel patterns of raised dots with their fingertips, often very fast.
A star-nosed mole has 22 fleshy fingers around its nose, covered in thousands of touch sensors. It finds food in dark tunnels by touch alone.
explanations.art: A cut-away of skin showing different little receptor shapes at different depths, each with a tiny icon: a feather, a pressing thumb, a buzzing phone and a bending finger.
explanations.context: Touch feels like one sense. This card shows that your skin really holds several kinds of receptor, each detecting something different.

explanations.definition: The 'hot' of chilli is not a taste. A chemical in chilli, called capsaicin, switches on the nerve endings that warn you of heat. Mint does the opposite and switches on the cold nerve endings.
explanations.description: Your mouth has nerve endings that warn you when something is hot enough to burn. They have a gate that opens at about 43 degrees Celsius. That is a little hotter than a hot bath. Capsaicin from chilli fits that gate and opens it too, even when the chilli is cold. So your brain gets the message 'burning!' That is why chilli makes you sweat and your face go red. In 1997 an American scientist, David Julius, found this gate by using chilli. He shared the 2021 Nobel Prize with Ardem Patapoutian. Menthol from mint opens the gate of the cold nerve endings. So mint feels cool, even in a warm mouth. Birds have a slightly different heat gate that capsaicin cannot open. So birds eat chillies without feeling any burn, and spread the seeds.
examples: Chilli on your fingers can make them burn too, because skin has the same heat nerve endings. That is why you must wash your hands before touching your eyes.
A cold glass of water does not stop the chilli burn for long. The capsaicin is still holding the gate open.
explanations.art: A green chilli and a mint leaf side by side. Below them is a nerve ending with a little gate, opened by a chilli key and glowing red, and another gate opened by a mint key glowing blue.
explanations.context: Is chilli a taste? This card explains why scientists say no, and what chilli really does to your mouth.

explanations.definition: Taste buds hold receptor cells that notice five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Every part of the tongue that has taste buds can notice all five.
explanations.description: Look at your tongue in a mirror. It is covered in tiny bumps. Inside many of them are taste buds, too small to see. Each taste bud is a bunch of about 50 to 100 taste cells. Food has to dissolve in spit first. Then its molecules reach the taste cells. Each kind of taste cell has receptors shaped to detect certain molecules, a bit like a lock that only a certain key fits. Sugar fits the sweet receptors. Salt and acid, like lemon, work on salty and sour cells. Bitter receptors detect many different molecules, and many poisons are bitter. So bitterness is partly a warning. Umami receptors detect glutamate, a molecule in tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese. A Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, named umami in 1908. Taste cells wear out and are replaced about every two weeks. That is why a burnt tongue heals.
examples: Sweet: gur, honey and ripe mango. Sour: imli, lemon and curd. Salty: salt and papad. Bitter: karela, neem and black coffee. Umami: tomato, mushroom and cheese.
Cats cannot taste sweet at all. In 2005 scientists found that the gene for their sweet receptor is broken.
explanations.art: A tongue with tiny bumps, a zoom into one bump showing a taste bud like a flower bud, and five small key-shaped molecules for the five tastes.
explanations.context: How does your tongue know that gur is sweet and karela is bitter? This card zooms in to the taste buds to find out.

explanations.concept: The tongue map that was never true
explanations.definition: The famous 'tongue map', with sweet only at the tip and bitter only at the back, is wrong. Every part of the tongue that has taste buds can taste every basic taste.
explanations.description: In 1901 a German scientist, David Hänig, tested people's tongues. He found that some parts were very slightly more sensitive to some tastes. The differences were tiny. In 1942 an American psychologist, Edwin Boring, redrew Hänig's results in a book. The drawing made the tiny differences look like separate zones. Other books copied it as a map, and it was printed in school books around the world. In 1974 another American scientist, Virginia Collings, tested it again carefully. She found every taste could be tasted all over the tongue. Later, scientists found taste receptors for every taste spread across the whole tongue. You can test it yourself with a cotton bud.
examples: Dab sugar water on the very back of your tongue. You can taste sweet there.
Dab a drop of karela juice on the tip. You can taste bitter there.
explanations.art: An old textbook page with a tongue split into coloured zones, crossed out, next to a tongue sprinkled all over with tiny taste buds of every colour.
explanations.context: Many grown-ups learned a tongue map at school. This card explains how a wrong map got into books, and how it was found out.

explanations.definition: Umami was named in 1908 by a Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda. For almost 100 years many scientists doubted it, until umami receptors were found in taste cells in 2000 and 2002.
explanations.description: In about 1907, a Japanese chemist called Kikunae Ikeda was eating tofu in a broth made from kombu, a kind of seaweed. He noticed a taste that was not sweet, sour, salty or bitter. He wanted to know what made it. He boiled down a large amount of kombu and found crystals of a substance called glutamate. In 1908 he named its taste umami, a Japanese word for a savoury, delicious taste. For most of the 1900s, many scientists outside Japan did not accept this. Their books said there were only four basic tastes. They said umami was just a mix of salty and the others. Ikeda's idea could only be settled by finding a receptor for it. In 2000, a team led by Nirupa Chaudhari and Stephen Roper found a receptor in taste cells that detects glutamate. In 2002, Charles Zuker's team found another. Umami had its own receptors, so it was a basic taste, just as Ikeda had said almost 100 years before.
examples: Ikeda found umami in kombu, a seaweed used to make broth in Japan. In Indian food, ripe tomatoes give a lot of umami.
For a long time, many books said there were four basic tastes. Now most scientists count five.
explanations.art: A Japanese chemist in about 1908 at a table with a bowl of seaweed broth and a dish of white crystals, and a modern tongue with five kinds of taste receptor beside it.
explanations.context: Umami is the newest of the five basic tastes. This card tells how a chemist in Japan found it, and why other scientists took nearly 100 years to agree.

explanations.description: Scientists agree on five basic tastes. Some think there may be more. To count as a basic taste, scientists want a receptor on the tongue that detects it, and a taste that feels different from all the others. Different people and traditions count differently.
examples: Some people say very fatty foods, like ghee, have their own taste, separate from their smell and feel.
Ayurveda counts six tastes, called rasas: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent.

perspectives.explanation: There are five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Each has its own receptors on the tongue.

perspectives.who: Richard Mattes and Cordelia Running, scientists in the USA, in 2015
perspectives.explanation: Fat may be a sixth basic taste. They called it 'oleogustus'. In their tests, people could pick out fat in food even when smell and feel were hidden. Other scientists are not yet convinced.

perspectives.who: The Ayurveda tradition of India, in books such as the Charaka Samhita
perspectives.explanation: Food has six rasas: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent. Pungent is like chilli or ginger. Astringent is the dry, puckering feeling of raw banana or strong tea. Scientists would say these two are touch feelings in the mouth, not taste-bud tastes. But they are real parts of eating.

explanations.art: Six small bowls in a row: gur, lemon, salt, a green chilli, karela and a raw banana, with a question mark over a seventh empty bowl holding ghee.
explanations.context: We say there are five basic tastes. This card asks whether there might be more, and shows how different people count them.

explanations.definition: Smells are molecules floating in the air. Smell receptor cells high up inside the nose detect them and send signals to the brain.
explanations.description: When you open a box of laddoos, molecules float off them into the air. You breathe some in. High up inside your nose is a patch of skin about the size of a postage stamp. It holds millions of smell receptor cells. Each cell has one kind of smell receptor, shaped to detect certain molecules. People have about 400 different kinds. Most smells are made of many molecules, so one smell switches on a pattern of receptors. Your brain reads the pattern, like reading a word from its letters. That is how 400 kinds of receptor can tell apart a huge number of smells. Two American scientists, Linda Buck and Richard Axel, found the smell receptors in 1991. They won the Nobel Prize in 2004. Smell signals go almost straight to the parts of the brain for feelings and memory. That may be why a smell can suddenly bring back a memory from long ago. Smell receptor cells are nerve cells, and they are replaced every month or two. Most nerve cells are never replaced.
examples: The smell of rain on dry earth has a name: petrichor. Part of it comes from a molecule called geosmin, made by bacteria in the soil. Bacteria are living things made of just one cell.
The smell of your grandmother's house, or a school classroom, can bring back a whole day in a flash.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a nose with smell molecules drifting up to a small patch high inside, and a zoom showing receptor cells catching different molecules, like hands catching different coloured balls.
explanations.context: How does the smell of a laddoo get from the box into your head? This card follows it up your nose to your brain.

explanations.definition: Flavour is taste plus smell, with touch and temperature too. Most of what we call the 'taste' of food is really smell.
explanations.description: When you chew, smell molecules from the food float up from the back of your mouth into your nose. You do not notice them going in. Your brain mixes them with the signals from your tongue. Then it makes the whole flavour seem to be in your mouth, even though much of it came from your nose. Your tongue only tells you sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Your nose tells you mango or guava, cardamom or cinnamon, fresh or burnt. So when your nose is blocked by a cold, food tastes flat. Pinch your nose and the spice in a spoon of sugar vanishes. Let go, and it comes back. Many people who caught COVID-19 lost their sense of smell for a while. They often said food had lost its taste.
examples: With a blocked nose, a spoon of sugar with elaichi tastes only sweet. Let go of your nose, and the elaichi appears.
Hot food usually smells stronger than cold food, because heat sends more molecules into the air.
explanations.art: A cut-away head showing a child chewing, with smell molecules rising from the back of the mouth up into the nose, and an arrow showing them joining the tongue's signals in the brain.
explanations.context: Remember pinching your nose while tasting a spoon of spiced sugar? This card explains why the spice disappeared.

explanations.concept: How good is the human nose?
explanations.description: People often say humans have a poor sense of smell. Scientists now argue about whether that is true. Dogs are far better at many smells. But the human nose may be much better than people think.
examples: A dog's nose has many millions more smell cells than yours. Trained dogs can follow a person's smell trail that is many hours old.
In one experiment, blindfolded people crawled across grass and followed a trail of chocolate smell with their noses.

perspectives.who: Paul Broca, a French brain scientist, in the 1800s, and many books since
perspectives.explanation: The smell part of the human brain is small compared with the rest of our brain. So our sense of smell must be weak.

perspectives.who: John McGann, an American brain scientist, in 2017
perspectives.explanation: That was a guess, not a test. The human smell part of the brain has about as many nerve cells as that of many other mammals. People can smell some molecules at tiny amounts, better than some animals.

perspectives.who: Andreas Keller and others, in 2014, and the scientists who checked their maths
perspectives.explanation: Keller's team calculated that people can tell apart at least a trillion smells. Other scientists showed that the number depends on how the maths is done. It might be much smaller or much bigger. Nobody knows the real number.

perspectives.who: Asifa Majid and Niclas Burenhult, language scientists, in 2014
perspectives.explanation: English speakers find smells hard to name. But the Jahai people of the Malaysian rainforest name smells as easily as colours. So naming smells may depend on practice and language, not on the nose.

explanations.art: A dog and a child side by side sniffing a trail across grass, with a question mark between them.
explanations.context: Is the human nose weak? This card shows how scientists are arguing about it, and what one rainforest people can do.

explanations.concept: How seeing works, in one card
explanations.definition: We see when light enters the eye and is detected by rods and cones in the retina. Each cone or rod has a molecule that changes shape when light hits it, and that starts a nerve signal.
explanations.description: Light bounces off things and into your eye through the black hole in the middle, the pupil. The clear front of the eye and the lens bend the light, so it makes a small, upside-down picture on the retina, the back wall of the eye. The retina has about 120 million rods and about 6 million cones. Rods work in dim light. Cones work in bright light and see colour. There are three kinds of cone. One kind detects mostly red light, one mostly green and one mostly blue. Your brain mixes their signals into every colour you see. Inside each rod and cone is a molecule that straightens out when one tiny particle of light hits it. That change starts the nerve signal. A rod can notice a single particle of light. About one million nerve threads carry the signals from each eye to the brain. The picture on the retina is upside down, but the brain makes sense of it, so you see the world the right way up. The unit 'How we see' goes much deeper into light and the eye.
examples: Stare at a bright red shape and then at a white wall. Your red cones are tired, so you see a green-blue ghost: an afterimage.
Dogs have only two kinds of cone. They see blues and yellows well, but red and green look alike to them.
explanations.art: A cut-away eye with light coming in, the upside-down picture on the retina, and a zoom showing rods and three colours of cone, one with a molecule straightening as a speck of light hits it.
explanations.context: Seeing is one of the best-known senses. This card explains in one go how light becomes a signal, so it can be compared with the other senses.

explanations.definition: The brain mixes the signals from all the senses into one world. What one sense tells it can change what another sense seems to say.
explanations.description: Your brain does not keep the senses in separate boxes. It mixes them. Flavour is one example: taste and smell mixed together. Here are more. In 1976 two scientists in England, Harry McGurk and John MacDonald, made a film of a face saying 'ga' while the sound said 'ba'. People heard 'da'. Their eyes changed what their ears heard. A ventriloquist's voice seems to come from the puppet's moving mouth, because your eyes pull the sound towards it. In 2004, two scientists in England, Massimiliano Zampini and Charles Spence, played people the sound of their own chip-crunching through headphones. When the crunch was made louder, the chips seemed fresher and crisper. Even the colour of a drink can change how sweet it seems. So the brain does not take each sense on its own. It makes its best guess about the world from all of them together.
examples: In a noisy place, you understand someone better when you can see their lips move.
Give people lemon sharbat coloured with orange food colour. Some of them say it tastes of orange.
explanations.art: A child eating crunchy chips while wearing headphones, with sound waves, a crunch, a taste and a smell all flowing into one bright thought bubble.
explanations.context: Each sense seems to work on its own. This card shows how the brain mixes them, and how one sense can change what another seems to tell you.

explanations.concept: When one sense is missing, the brain finds another way
explanations.definition: When a person cannot use one sense, the brain often puts the other senses to work in new ways. It can even use brain parts that would normally be for the missing sense.
explanations.description: Brains can change with use. Think of people who have been blind from birth. In their brains, the parts normally used for seeing get used for touch and hearing instead. In 1996 a team in the USA, led by a Japanese scientist, Norihiro Sadato, scanned blind people reading Braille. The 'seeing' part of their brains was busy while their fingers read. Some blind people find their way by making tongue clicks and listening to the echoes, like bats. Daniel Kish, who lost both eyes as a baby, does this so well that he rides a bicycle. In 2011, Lore Thaler and her team in Canada studied expert blind clickers. The seeing part of their brains was busy while they listened to echoes. Their ears are not better than other people's. Their brains have learned to use the sounds more.
examples: Louis Braille lost his sight as a small boy in France. At about 15 years old, he invented the raised-dot writing that blind people around the world read with their fingertips.
Helen Keller could neither see nor hear. In 1887 her teacher, Anne Sullivan, spelled 'w-a-t-e-r' into one of her hands while water ran over the other. Helen understood that things have names.
explanations.art: A girl reading a Braille book with her fingertips, and beside her a young man clicking his tongue with gentle curved echo lines bouncing back from a wall.
explanations.context: What happens when someone cannot see or hear? This card shows how brains find new ways to sense the world.

explanations.concept: Every animal lives in its own sense-world
explanations.definition: Each kind of animal senses only some parts of the world. The world as one animal senses it is called its Umwelt. No animal senses everything.
explanations.description: A German scientist, Jakob von Uexküll, gave us the word Umwelt more than 100 years ago. A honeybee sees ultraviolet light, which we cannot see. Many flowers have ultraviolet stripes that lead the bee to their nectar. A bat fills the dark with squeaks too high for us, and hears the echoes. A pit viper has two small pits on its face that feel the warmth of a mouse in total darkness. An elephant hears rumbles far too low for us, and may feel them through its feet. A housefly and a butterfly taste with their feet. A catfish has taste buds all over its skin, so its whole body tastes the water. An octopus tastes with its suckers. A silk moth can smell a female moth from far away. Our own Umwelt is just one of millions. An Indian scientist, Obaid Siddiqi, studied how fruit flies taste and smell. He showed that the genes of a tiny fly can teach us how senses and nerves work.
examples: Crickets have their ears on their front legs.
Mosquitoes find you partly by smelling the breath and sweat you give off.
explanations.art: One garden drawn as four sense-worlds: a bee seeing ultraviolet stripes on flowers, a bat hearing echoes, a snake seeing a glowing warm mouse, and a fly tasting a mango with its feet.
explanations.context: Humans sense only part of the world. This card shows what some other animals sense that we cannot.

explanations.definition: Different people's senses are not exactly the same. Some people taste bitterness more strongly, some smell certain molecules differently, and some see colours differently.
explanations.description: About 8 in every 100 boys and men, and about 1 in every 200 girls and women, see some colours differently from most people. Usually red and green look alike to them. An American scientist, Linda Bartoshuk, found that some people are 'supertasters'. They have more taste buds and find bitter foods, like karela, much more bitter. For some people, fresh dhania leaves taste like soap. This is partly because of their genes. So when two people taste the same chutney, they may not taste quite the same thing. Neither one is wrong.
examples: You might love karela while your brother can hardly eat it. Your tongues may really be different.
A colour-blind child may find it hard to tell a ripe red tomato from a green one by colour alone.
explanations.art: Two children tasting from the same bowl of green chutney, one smiling and one pulling a face, with different thought bubbles above them.
explanations.context: Does everyone taste and see the same thing? This card shows that people's senses really differ, and that this is normal.

explanations.description: Scientists can follow a sense all the way from a ripe mango to electric signals in the brain. But here is the mystery. Why does it feel like anything at all? Why are some signals the warm yellow of a mango, and others its sweet smell? Scientists do not yet know. Some call this the hardest question about the mind.
examples: You cannot know for sure that the red you see is the same as the red your friend sees. You both call it 'red'.
A bat's echoes must feel like something to a bat. Can we ever imagine what?

perspectives.explanation: Experience is something the brain does. As we learn more about how brain cells work together, we will understand how signals become seeing and tasting.

perspectives.who: David Chalmers, an Australian philosopher, in 1995
perspectives.explanation: Explaining what brain cells do is one problem. Explaining why it feels like something is a different, much harder problem. He called it 'the hard problem'. It is still open.

perspectives.who: Thomas Nagel, an American philosopher, in 1974
perspectives.explanation: He asked, 'What is it like to be a bat?' Even if we knew everything about a bat's brain, we might still not know what its echoes feel like to it.

perspectives.who: Some philosophers, such as Philip Goff
perspectives.explanation: Maybe a tiny bit of awareness is part of everything, all the way down. This idea is called panpsychism. Most scientists do not accept it, but nobody has disproved it.

explanations.art: A ripe mango, then a line of sparks going into a brain, then a big glowing question mark where the colour yellow and the sweet smell should appear.
explanations.context: This unit followed each sense down to electric signals. This card asks the question nobody can answer yet: how signals become the taste of a mango.

agreed.text: Every sense works by receptor cells detecting something from the world and turning it into nerve signals for the brain.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can record the tiny electric signals in single receptor cells and nerves, for example in a rod cell when light hits it.

agreed.text: There are five basic tastes, and every part of the tongue with taste buds can taste all of them.
agreed.evidence: Careful taste tests since 1974, and the discovery of the taste receptors themselves, spread across the whole tongue.

agreed.text: Most of the flavour of food comes from smell.
agreed.evidence: Pinch your nose and you can no longer tell cinnamon sugar from plain sugar. People who lose their sense of smell say food has lost its taste.

agreed.text: In people, the hair cells of the inner ear do not grow back, so loud noise can cause hearing loss that lasts.
agreed.evidence: Doctors find damaged hair cells in the ears of people who worked for years in loud places, like factories.

agreed.text: Many animals sense things humans cannot, such as ultraviolet light, echoes, very low rumbles and the warmth of prey in the dark.
agreed.evidence: Careful tests: bees trained to visit ultraviolet patterns, bats catching moths in the dark, snakes striking at warm targets with their eyes covered.

chart.title: The highest sound each animal can hear (about)
chart.y: Highest sound heard (thousands of vibrations each second)
chart.note: Numbers are rounded. Some bats hear even higher.

challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, in his book On the Soul, about 2,350 years ago. Many school books still say it.
challenging.for: Five sense organs are easy to see: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. Many traditions, in India too, counted five.
challenging.against: Scientists count many more. Balance, knowing where your hands are with your eyes shut, feeling hot and cold, pain, hunger and thirst all have their own receptors. Depending on how you count, there are somewhere between about a dozen and over 30.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that we have exactly five senses.

challenging.claim: Different parts of the tongue taste different tastes: sweet at the tip, bitter at the back.
challenging.who: The 'tongue map', printed in school books for much of the 1900s
challenging.for: A study in 1901 did find tiny differences in how sensitive parts of the tongue were.
challenging.against: The differences were tiny, and a 1942 drawing made them look like zones. Tests in 1974 and the discovery of taste receptors showed every part of the tongue with taste buds tastes everything.
challenging.context: This card is about the tongue map that many grown-ups learned at school.

challenging.claim: Humans have a poor sense of smell.
challenging.who: Many books, going back to the French brain scientist Paul Broca in the 1800s
challenging.for: Dogs, rats and elephants have many more kinds of smell receptor than we do, and dogs follow trails we cannot.
challenging.against: In 2017 the scientist John McGann argued that this was based on a guess, not tests. People can smell some molecules at tiny amounts, and can follow a smell trail across grass.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the human nose is really weak.

challenging.claim: There are six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent.
challenging.who: The Ayurveda tradition of India, for example in the Charaka Samhita
challenging.for: These six really are six different feelings when we eat, and they are useful for cooking and describing food.
challenging.against: Scientists count five tastes that the taste buds detect. Pungent, like chilli, and astringent, like raw banana, are detected by touch and pain nerve endings in the mouth, not by taste buds. And umami is missing from the six.
challenging.context: Ayurveda, India's old system of medicine, counts six tastes. This card compares that with how scientists count.

challenging.claim: Umami is not a real taste. It is just a mix of the other tastes.
challenging.who: Many scientists outside Japan, for most of the 1900s
challenging.for: Umami foods are often also salty, and it is hard to taste umami on its own.
challenging.against: Around the year 2000, scientists found receptors on the tongue that detect glutamate, the umami molecule. So Kikunae Ikeda, who named umami in 1908, had been right all along.
challenging.context: This card is about umami, the savoury taste, and why it took nearly 100 years to be accepted.

challenging.claim: Blind people have better ears than sighted people.
challenging.for: Many blind people notice sounds that sighted people miss, and some can find their way with echoes.
challenging.against: Their ears are usually just the same. What changes is the brain. With practice it learns to get more out of the same sounds, and even uses the parts normally used for seeing.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief about blind people's hearing.

challenging.claim: Eating lots of carrots gives you night vision.
challenging.who: A story spread in Britain during the Second World War
challenging.for: Carrots have a substance the body turns into vitamin A. Without enough vitamin A, people really do get night blindness.
challenging.against: Extra carrots do not give a healthy person better night vision than normal. The story was spread partly to hide the fact that British pilots were using radar.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story that carrots help you see in the dark.

big_questions.q: Your brain sits in the dark, and only gets electric signals. So where is the colour of a mango? In the mango, in your eye, or in your brain?
big_questions.hint: Think about a bee. It sees ultraviolet patterns on flowers that you cannot. Which flower is the real one?

big_questions.q: If every sense sends the same kind of electric signal, why does seeing feel so different from hearing?
big_questions.hint: Think about where each signal goes in the brain. Is that enough to explain it?

big_questions.q: Is there anything all around us right now that no animal on Earth can sense?
big_questions.hint: We cannot sense ultraviolet light or radio waves, but our machines can. What else might be there?

big_questions.q: If your friend tastes the same chutney as you, do you taste the same thing? How could you ever know?
big_questions.hint: Some people taste dhania as soap. How would you describe a taste to someone who has never had it?

big_questions.q: Does a person who is blind live in a smaller world, or a different one?
big_questions.hint: Think of Daniel Kish, who rides a bicycle using echoes. What does his world have that yours might not?

big_questions.q: Why do you think our senses stop noticing things that stay the same, like the feel of your clothes?
big_questions.hint: What would it be like if you felt your shirt every second of the day?

big_questions.q: Hair cells in birds grow back, but not in people. Why might living things be so different?
big_questions.hint: Scientists are still trying to find out. What would you test?

big_questions.q: Is a smell that nobody is smelling still a smell? Is a sound that nobody hears still a sound?
big_questions.hint: A tree falls in an empty forest. The air shakes. Is that a sound?

big_questions.q: A wrong tongue map stayed in school books for more than 30 years. Why do wrong ideas get copied, and how can we find them out?
big_questions.hint: Who could have tested it with a cotton bud and some sugar?

big_questions.q: Who is doing the sensing? Is it your eyes, your brain, or you?
big_questions.hint: Close your eyes. Something is still noticing the sounds around you. What is it?

story.title: Tara Listens to the Walls
story.note: Tara, Arjun, Chhotu and the house are made up. Tongue-click echolocation is real: some blind people, such as Daniel Kish in the USA, use it to walk, hike and even ride bicycles, and scientists have studied it since the 1940s.
text: Arjun came to his cousin's house in Lucknow for the summer holidays. It was an old house with too many rooms. The rooms were joined by long, dim passages, and an open courtyard sat in the middle.

His cousin Tara was ten, a year older than him. She had been blind since she was born. On the train, Arjun had worried about what to say to her. He had imagined her world as an endless dark room, with nothing in it at all.

But Tara walked through the passages faster than he did. As she walked, she made a small sound with her tongue against the roof of her mouth. Tock. Tock. Like a drop of water falling into a steel bucket.
'Why do you keep doing that?' Arjun asked on the first day.
'I'm listening to the walls,' said Tara.
Arjun laughed, because he thought it was a joke. Tara did not laugh. She just went on clicking, and turned left exactly where the passage turned left.

Over the next few days, Arjun watched her. She knew the kitchen by the sharp smell of mustard oil, and the terrace by the mogra flowers in their pots. In the courtyard she took off her chappals, because the marble was cool and told her feet where she was. She found the brass knob of her grandfather's door without reaching for it twice. Arjun began to feel that Tara lived in a full house, and he lived in an empty one.
Then came the evening of the storm.

It started with a game of hide and seek. Chhotu, Arjun's little brother, was four, and he was very good at hiding. He wore silver anklets with tiny bells, so the grown-ups could always hear where he was. That evening, nobody could find him.

At first it was funny. Then the sky turned the colour of a bruise, and the rain came down on the roof like a thousand drums. With a click and a sigh, the lights went out. The inverter had been broken for a week. The whole house fell into a darkness so thick that Arjun could not see his own hand.

Everyone began to shout at once. 'Chhotu! Chhotu!' Mamaji switched on the torch of his phone. It made one small bright circle on the wall, and everything outside the circle became even blacker. Mami's phone had no charge. Nani was calling from upstairs. The rain roared. Arjun ran down the passage towards where he thought the storeroom was. He hit a doorframe with his shoulder and sat down hard on the floor, his eyes wide open and useless.
Then a voice cut through the noise. It was not loud. It was very calm.
'Everyone,' said Tara. 'Please stop talking.'
Something in her voice made them do it. One by one, the shouting stopped. Mamaji switched off his torch. Now there was only the rain, and the dark, and everyone breathing.
Tara stood very still in the middle of the passage. Arjun could just make out her shape. She turned her head slowly to the right, and then slowly to the left, the way a bird does.
'There,' she whispered. 'He moved in his sleep. Left, and low down.'
Arjun had heard nothing. He strained his ears until they hurt. Nothing but rain.
Tara found his hand in the dark. 'Close your eyes,' she said.
'It's dark anyway. What's the point?'
'Your eyes are still trying,' said Tara. 'They're shouting at you. Close them, so you can hear.'

Arjun closed his eyes. At first nothing changed. Then, under the drumming of the rain, he heard it. Chhm. The tiniest sound, like a grain of rice dropped on a plate. He turned his head the way Tara had. When his left ear faced the sound, it was a little clearer. When he turned away, it faded.
'Left,' he breathed.
'Left,' agreed Tara.

She led him by the hand, and she clicked. Tock. Tock. Arjun began to hear what she heard. When they walked close to a wall, the click came back sharp and quick, as if the wall were clicking back. In the open courtyard, the click floated away and was gone. At a doorway, it changed again. It became hollow, as if the sound were falling into a well.

'The storeroom,' said Tara. Arjun smelled it before she said it: old rice sacks, dust and camphor. His fingers touched something cold and smooth. It was one of the big steel trunks. Tara knelt. Behind the last trunk, curled up on a folded quilt, Chhotu was fast asleep with his thumb in his mouth. As Tara touched his foot, his anklet chimed once more.

At that moment the lights came back on. Everyone appeared at the storeroom door at once, blinking and squinting, their hands over their eyes. Mami scooped Chhotu up and he woke, very cross, and asked why everyone was looking at him. Tara simply stood there. For her, nothing had changed at all.

That night, Arjun lay in bed with his eyes shut. The rain had stopped. The house was quiet. He made a small sound with his tongue. Tock. From the wall beside his head, faintly, something answered, like a hand cupped close to his ear.
He lay very still and listened. The room was not empty after all. It never had been.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the world Arjun experiences is not in his eyes. It is built by his brain from whatever signals arrive. When his eyes gave him nothing, they were still 'shouting', and Tara teaches him to let them rest so his ears can work. Then he hears what she hears. Two ears comparing a tiny sound tell him its direction. Echoes from her clicks tell him how near the walls are. Smell and touch tell him where he is. Tara does not have better ears than him. She has trained her brain to use them, and to mix all her senses into one full world.
ask: Why could Tara hear Chhotu's anklet when everyone else could not?
Why did Tara tell Arjun to close his eyes, even though it was already dark?
How did turning his head help Arjun find which way the sound came from?
What did Tara's clicks sound like near a wall, in the open courtyard and at a doorway?
At the start, Arjun thought Tara lived in an empty dark room. At the end, what did he think?
art: An old house in Lucknow with a marble courtyard, and a girl walking confidently down a dim passage, clicking her tongue.
Tara barefoot on the cool courtyard marble, smelling the mogra pots on the terrace above.
The storm, the lights out, one small phone-torch circle on a wall and dark shapes of worried people.
Arjun with his eyes shut, head turned to the left, and Tara holding his hand, clicking.
Chhotu asleep on a quilt behind steel trunks in a storeroom, his silver anklet catching the first light as the power comes back.

games.title: Super-Sense Pairs

printables.title: 24 cards to cut out: 12 animal cards and 12 super-sense cards
items: SENSE: I taste with my feet.
SENSE: My ears are on my front legs.
SENSE: I catch mice in total darkness, by sound alone.
SENSE: My nose has 22 fleshy fingers for touching.
SENSE: My whole skin is covered in taste buds.
SENSE: I see ultraviolet stripes on flowers.
SENSE: I feel the warmth of a mouse in the dark.
SENSE: I hear rumbles far too low for you.
SENSE: I squeak and listen for echoes.
SENSE: I smell a mate from far away.
SENSE: I cannot taste sweet at all.
SENSE: I eat chillies and feel no burn.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: My best time or fewest turns

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and lay them face down in 4 rows of 6.
On your turn, turn over any two cards and read them out loud.
If you turn over an animal and the super-sense that belongs to it, you have a pair. To keep it, say which human sense it is most like. For example, 'a fly tasting with its feet is like taste'.
If they do not match, turn them face down again. Try to remember where they are.
With friends or a parent: take turns. The player with the most pairs at the end wins.
Playing alone: count your turns. Write your number on the score sheet. Next time, try to finish in fewer turns.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Lay them face down in 4 rows of 6.
flow.say: Every animal lives in its own world of senses. In this game, you match each animal to its super-sense. Turn over two cards at a time.
flow.kid: Shuffle the 24 cards. Lay them face down in 4 rows of 6. Each animal has a matching super-sense card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Super-Sense Pairs. It is a memory game where you match animals to the things they can sense that we cannot.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together. Turn over the Bat card and the echoes card, and read them out.
flow.say: Here is a practice pair: a bat, and 'I squeak and listen for echoes'. Which of your senses is that most like?
flow.kid: Practice pair: a bat, and 'I squeak and listen for echoes'. Which of your senses is it most like?

check.q: A bat squeaks and listens for echoes to find moths in the dark. Which human sense is that most like?
options: Hearing
Smell
Taste
Touch
check.why: The bat is using its ears. It sends out a squeak and hears it bounce back off a moth. Some blind people do the same with tongue clicks. If you picked touch, that is an interesting thought. Echoes are a bit like touching things from far away with sound.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over two cards. 2. When someone finds a pair, they say which human sense it is most like, and keep the pair. 3. If you are playing alone, count your turns.
flow.say: Your turn. Turn over two. Is it a pair? If it is, which human sense is it like?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. A pair? Say which of your senses it is like. Then keep it. Not a pair? Turn them back and remember them.
flow.parent: The parrot card is a trick. Chilli 'heat' is not a taste. It is the heat-warning nerve endings, so it is most like touch. The cat card is taste. The pit viper is most like touch, because we feel warmth with our skin.

flow.do: 1. Count the pairs, or the turns if playing alone. 2. Talk about which super-sense each player would most like to have.
flow.say: If you could have one of these super-senses for a day, which would you choose? What would you notice in our house that you can't notice now?
flow.kid: Count your pairs or your turns. Which super-sense would you choose for one day? What would you notice at home?
flow.think: These animals are sensing things that are really there, all around us. What might be all around you right now that you cannot sense?

games.context: This is a memory card game about animal senses. You match 12 animals to the things they can sense that we cannot, and say which human sense each one is like.

games.title: Kim's Game for Five Senses

printables.title: Score sheet for five rounds
items: Round 1, Sight: what is missing from the tray?
Round 2, Hearing: name the kitchen sounds
Round 4, Touch: name the things in the bag

printables.title: Five round cards
items: SIGHT: Look at the tray for one minute. Then close your eyes. One thing will vanish.
HEARING: Turn your back. Name each kitchen sound.
SMELL: Eyes shut. Waft each katori towards your nose and name the smell.
TOUCH: Put your hand in the bag. Name each thing without looking.
TASTE: Eyes shut. Name the basic taste: sweet, sour, salty, bitter or umami.

rules: This game comes from a famous book called Kim, by Rudyard Kipling, published in 1901 and set in India. In it, a boy called Kim is trained to remember things on a tray by looking for one minute.
There are five rounds, one for each sense. One person is the game-master and sets up each round. The others play.
In each round, you score 1 point for each thing you name correctly.
Players can take turns being the game-master.
Add up the points after all five rounds. The highest total wins. Then talk about which sense was easiest, and which was hardest.

flow.do: 1. Sight round: put 10 small things on a tray. For example, a spoon, a key, a coin, an elaichi pod and a bangle. Add a pencil, an eraser, a button, a leaf and a hair clip. 2. Players look for one minute. 3. They close their eyes. Take one thing away. 4. They open their eyes and say what is missing. 5. Do it three times.
flow.say: Look at the tray for one whole minute. Try to remember everything. Then close your eyes, and I'll make one thing vanish.
flow.kid: Look at the tray for one minute. Remember everything. Close your eyes. Open them. What is missing?
flow.context: This is the first round of Kim's Game for Five Senses. Players look at a tray of things and remember them. It is based on a game in the book Kim, set in India.

flow.do: 1. Hearing round: players turn their backs. 2. Make 5 kitchen sounds, one at a time. Pour water. Shake a box of matches. Stir a spoon in a steel glass. Tear paper. Click the gas lighter with the gas off. 3. Players write or say what each one is.
flow.say: Backs to me. Listen carefully. What is making each sound?
flow.kid: Turn your back. Listen to each sound. What made it?
flow.parent: Make the sounds at the same distance each time. Do not use the gas stove itself.

flow.do: 1. Smell round: put a small amount of 5 smelly things in covered katoris. For example, jeera, laung, a slice of ginger, a curry leaf and a little coffee. 2. Players shut their eyes. 3. Lift one lid at a time. They waft the air towards their nose with their hand and name it.
flow.say: Eyes shut. Wave the air from the bowl towards your nose, gently. Don't sniff hard. What is it?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Wave the air towards your nose with your hand. Don't sniff hard. What is it?
flow.parent: Wafting is safer than sniffing hard. It is also how scientists smell things in a lab. Many people know a smell but cannot find its name. That is normal.

flow.do: 1. Touch round: put 5 things in a cloth bag or pillowcase. For example, a coin, a key, a rubber band, a dry rajma bean and a button. 2. Each player puts one hand in and names each thing without looking.
flow.say: Hand in the bag. No peeking. Feel each thing. What is it?
flow.kid: Put one hand in the bag. Don't look. Feel each thing. What is it?

ask.q: Which part of your hand did you use most to feel?
good: The tips of my fingers, because they feel the most detail.

flow.do: 1. Taste round: put a few drops of 4 tastes on separate spoons. Use sugar water, salt water, lemon water, and karela juice or very strong tea. 2. Players shut their eyes and name the basic taste of each. 3. Add up all the points.
flow.say: Eyes shut. Tell me the basic taste: sweet, sour, salty, bitter or umami?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Taste each spoon. Is it sweet, sour, salty, bitter or umami?

check.q: In the taste round, which spoon tastes bitter?
options: Sugar water
Salt water
Lemon water
Karela juice
check.why: Karela is the bitter one. Many poisons in nature are bitter, so bitterness is partly a warning taste. Lemon is sour, not bitter. People often mix up sour and bitter, so it helps to taste them side by side.

games.context: This is a five-round memory and guessing game. Each round uses a different sense: sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste. It grows out of a game in Rudyard Kipling's book Kim, set in India.
