items.p: What does a receptor do?
opts: It stores food for the body
It notices one kind of thing, like light or a push, and makes a nerve signal
items.why: A receptor is a special cell that notices one kind of thing and turns it into a tiny electric signal. Picking 'makes sounds' usually mixes up catching a sound with making one.

items.p: Nerves carry tiny electric ____ from the senses to the brain.
items.why: Every sense sends its messages to the brain as tiny pulses of electricity called nerve signals.

items.p: Match each sense organ to what it detects.
items.why: Each sense organ detects one kind of thing from the world and has receptors built for it.

items.p: Put the path of a sound in order, from outside to the brain: eardrum, cochlea, ear flap, three tiny bones, ear canal, nerve.
items.why: The ear flap collects the sound. It goes down the ear canal and shakes the eardrum. Three tiny bones pass the shaking to the cochlea. Hair cells there make signals, and the nerve carries them to the brain.
items.art: A cut-away ear with the six parts marked by small numbered circles, without labels.

items.p: The smallest bone in your body is inside your ear.
items.why: True. The stirrup, one of the three tiny bones behind the eardrum, is about the size of a grain of rice.

items.p: In the Point at the Sound test, which sounds are hardest to point to?
opts: Sounds straight in front or straight behind
items.why: A sound straight in front or behind reaches both ears at the same moment and loudness. So the brain has no difference to compare. Picking 'left' or 'right' usually means forgetting that the brain uses the difference between the two ears.

items.p: In the Two-Point Test, which place felt two points closest together?
items.why: Fingertips have touch receptors packed very close together, so they feel the most detail. Picking 'all the same' usually means thinking all skin is alike. The test shows it is not.

items.p: Sort these foods by their main basic taste.
items.why: Sweet foods have sugars. Sour foods have acids. Salty foods have salt. Bitter foods, like karela and neem, have bitter molecules. Ripe tomatoes have glutamate, which gives umami.

items.p: The tip of your tongue can only taste sweet things.
items.why: False. That is the old tongue map, and it is wrong. Every part of the tongue with taste buds can taste all five basic tastes.

items.p: Why does food taste flat when you have a blocked nose?
opts: Most flavour is really smell, and the smell cannot reach your nose
A cold makes food less salty
items.why: Your tongue still tastes sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. But the smells from food cannot float up into a blocked nose, and most flavour is smell. Picking 'tongue stops working' usually means thinking all taste comes from the tongue.

items.p: Taste plus smell together make ____.
items.why: Flavour is taste from the tongue mixed with smell from the nose, plus touch and temperature.

items.p: Which cells in your eye see colour?
items.why: Cones see colour, in bright light. Rods work in dim light but see no colour. Hair cells are in the ear. Picking rods is a common mix-up, because the two words go together.

items.p: Which animal tastes with its feet?
items.why: Houseflies and butterflies have taste hairs on their feet, so they taste what they land on. Picking 'cat' may come from remembering that cats are unusual tasters. Cats cannot taste sweet.

items.p: Your friend says, 'We have exactly five senses.' What would you tell them? Give one example.
items.a: We have more than five. For example, balance tells us if we are tipping over, and we can feel where our hands are with our eyes shut.
items.why: The five senses are an old list. Scientists count many more, each with its own receptors.

items.p: In Senses You Forgot You Had, standing on one foot was much harder with your eyes shut. Why?
opts: Your legs get weaker when your eyes are shut
Your brain balances using your eyes, your inner ears and your muscle sensors together, and you took one away
Your ears stop working when your eyes are shut
items.why: Balance uses three senses at once: your eyes, the balance organs in your inner ears and the stretch sensors in your muscles. Shutting your eyes takes one away, so the other two have to do all the work. Picking 'balance only uses the eyes' is wrong, because you could still balance for a few seconds with your eyes shut.

items.p: Draw the path of a smell: from a hot jalebi, up your nose, to your brain. Label the smell molecules, the smell receptors and the nerve.
items.a: Molecules float from the jalebi into the nose. They reach receptor cells high inside the nose. A nerve carries the signal to the brain.
items.why: Smells are molecules. Receptors high in the nose detect them, and nerves carry the signals to the brain.
items.art: An outline of a face from the side next to a jalebi, with empty space for the child to draw.

items.p: Look at the chart from the Point at the Sound test. The child found 7 sounds with two ears and 4 with one ear blocked. What does this show?

chart.title: Sounds found correctly, out of 8 (made-up results)

items.a: Two ears are better for finding where a sound comes from. The child found 3 more sounds with two ears. The brain compares the two ears.
items.why: With one ear blocked, the brain has much less to compare, so pointing gets worse.

items.p: A signal from your eye and a signal from your ear both reach your brain. How are they different?
opts: One is light and one is sound
They are the same kind of electric signal, but they arrive at different parts of the brain
The eye signal is much faster
items.why: No light or sound reaches the brain. Every sense sends the same kind of electric signal. The brain knows which is which by where it arrives. Picking 'one is light' is the most common idea, and it is the surprise of this unit.

items.p: What happens to a hair cell in your cochlea when sound reaches it?
opts: Its tiny tuft bends, gates open, and it makes a nerve signal
items.why: Sound ripples the liquid in the cochlea. The tufts on the hair cells bend. That opens tiny gates, and the cell makes a signal. Picking 'it makes a sound back' mixes up hearing with echoes.

items.p: If loud noise breaks the hair cells in a person's ear, new ones grow back in a few weeks.
items.why: False. In people, broken hair cells do not grow back. That is why hearing lost to loud noise stays lost. Birds can grow new ones, and scientists are studying how.

items.p: Chilli feels 'hot' in your mouth. What is really happening?
opts: The chilli is really very hot
A chemical in chilli opens the gates of the nerve endings that warn of burning
Chilli is a sixth basic taste
items.why: Capsaicin, the chemical in chilli, opens the same gates that open at burning heat. So your brain gets the message 'hot', even from cold chilli. Picking 'sixth taste' is understandable, but chilli is caught by heat nerve endings, not taste buds.

items.p: Birds eat chillies and do not feel the burn. Why?
opts: Birds' heat gate is a slightly different shape, so capsaicin cannot open it
items.why: Capsaicin fits the heat gate in mammals, like us, but not the bird version. So birds eat chillies happily and spread their seeds. Picking 'cannot taste anything' is wrong, because birds do have taste buds.

items.p: The savoury, meaty basic taste of tomatoes and mushrooms is called ____.
items.why: Kikunae Ikeda named umami in 1908. It is the taste of glutamate.

items.p: People have about 400 kinds of smell receptor. How can they tell apart so many more than 400 smells?
opts: Each smell switches on a different pattern of receptors, like letters making words
Each receptor smells 1,000 things on its own
items.why: Most smells are mixes of molecules that switch on several kinds of receptor at once. The brain reads the pattern, the way you read a word from its letters. Picking '400 smells only' means thinking one receptor gives one smell.

items.p: A single rod cell in your eye can notice one tiny particle of light.
items.why: True. Inside each rod is a molecule that changes shape when one particle of light hits it. That starts a nerve signal.

items.p: In the Blue Mango activity, you stared at a blue mango and then saw a yellow one on white paper. What made the yellow?
opts: Tired blue cones, so the other cones sent more signals
items.why: Staring tired out your blue cones. On white paper, the other cones sent more signals, so your brain saw yellow. Picking 'yellow ink' shows how real afterimages feel, but the paper was blank.

items.p: In the Fading Coin activity, you stopped feeling a still coin, but felt it again when it moved. What does this show?
opts: Skin only works when you look at it
Touch receptors stop working for ever
items.why: Many receptors fire when something changes and go quiet when nothing does. That is why you stop noticing your clothes. Picking 'stop working for ever' is wrong, because you felt the nudge at once.

items.p: Match each animal to its super-sense.
pairs: feels the warmth of a mouse in the dark
items.why: Each animal lives in its own sense-world, called its Umwelt. These animals detect things humans cannot.

items.p: In the McGurk experiment, people watch a face saying 'ga' while the sound says 'ba'. Many hear 'da'. What does this show?
opts: The brain mixes what the eyes see with what the ears hear
items.why: The brain makes its best guess using all the senses together, so the moving lips change what you hear. Picking 'ears are broken' is wrong. Close your eyes, and you hear 'ba' correctly.

items.p: Some blind people find their way with tongue clicks. Explain how this works, using the word echo.
items.a: They click and listen for the echo, the sound bouncing back. A quick sharp echo means a wall is close. Their brain learns to build a picture from the echoes.
items.why: This is echolocation, the same idea bats use. Expert clickers even use the seeing parts of their brains for it.

items.p: In the Hold Your Nose test, one child named a spice even with her nose pinched. What is the best thing to check?
opts: That her nose was fully shut, and the spice was well mixed
That she has a special tongue
items.why: A nose not fully pinched lets some smell through. Lumps of spice can be felt by the tongue too. A good scientist checks the test was fair before deciding. Picking 'the test failed' gives up too soon.

items.p: Your brother loves karela, but you find it far too bitter. Is one of you wrong? Explain.
items.a: Neither of us is wrong. People's tongues really differ. Some people, called supertasters, have more taste buds and find bitter things much more bitter.
items.why: People's senses really differ. Linda Bartoshuk found supertasters, who taste bitterness more strongly.

items.p: Johannes Müller noticed that pressing on the eye's nerve makes people see flashes of light. What does this tell us?
opts: The eye makes its own light
A nerve from the eye can only say 'light', whatever starts its signal
Pressing the eye is good for it
items.why: A signal on the seeing pathway is read as light, whatever caused it. So the kind of sense depends on where the signal goes. Picking 'the eye makes its own light' is a natural guess, but there is no light. It is just a signal.

items.p: Light reaches your brain through your eyes.
items.why: False. Light stops at the retina. Only electric signals travel along the nerve to the brain. Inside the skull it is dark.

items.p: A barn owl's two ears are at different heights on its head. How does this help it?
opts: It can hear only high sounds
It can tell whether a sound is above or below, not just left or right
items.why: With ears at different heights, a sound from below reaches one ear slightly differently from the other. So the owl's brain can work out up and down too, and catch a mouse in the dark.

items.p: The tongue map stayed in school books for many years. Which person showed in 1974 that it was wrong?
items.why: Virginia Collings repeated the tests carefully in 1974 and found every taste all over the tongue. Edwin Boring drew the graph in 1942 that started the mistake. Ikeda named umami.

items.p: Why do you think a wrong idea, like the tongue map, can stay in books for a long time? How could you check an idea for yourself?
items.a: Books copy from other books, and people trust what is printed. I could test it myself, with a fair test, for example with cotton buds and sugar water on different parts of my tongue.
items.why: Science means checking ideas against what really happens, not just trusting a famous book.

items.p: Ayurveda counts six tastes, including pungent, like ginger, and astringent, like raw banana. How would a scientist explain those two?
opts: They are detected by taste buds like the others
They are touch and pain feelings in the mouth, not taste-bud tastes
items.why: Pungent and astringent are real feelings when we eat, but they come from nerve endings for heat, pain and touch, not from taste buds. Picking 'they do not exist' is unfair. People feel them clearly.

items.p: Scientists argue about how many smells people can tell apart. Why is it so hard to count?
opts: The answer depends on how the maths is done, and nobody can test every smell
Noses are too small to study
items.why: There are far too many possible mixtures to test one by one. So scientists estimate, and different methods give very different numbers. Picking 'nobody has tried' is wrong. Many teams have tried.

items.p: Asifa Majid found that the Jahai people of Malaysia name smells as easily as colours. What does this suggest?
opts: Naming smells may depend on language and practice
English has no smell words at all
items.why: Their noses are like everyone's. Their language has many words just for smells, and they practise using them. Picking 'bigger noses' means looking for the answer in the body, when it may be in practice and words.

items.p: In the Train Your Nose project, why test a family member who did not practise?
opts: To compare, so you know if practice made the difference and not luck
To make the jars smell stronger
items.why: Comparing with someone who did not practise helps show whether the practice really made the difference. Scientists call this a comparison or a control.

items.p: Blind people's brains use their 'seeing' parts for touch and hearing. What does this tell you about brains?
items.a: Brains can change. If one sense is missing, the brain can give its parts a new job for other senses.
items.why: Norihiro Sadato's team found the seeing part of the brain busy in blind people reading Braille. Brains change with use.

items.p: Two people tasting the same chutney always taste exactly the same thing.
items.why: False. People's tongues and noses differ. For example, some people find dhania tastes like soap, partly because of their genes.

items.p: A bee sees ultraviolet stripes on a flower that you cannot see. Which is the 'real' flower: the one you see or the one the bee sees? Explain what you think.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer is good. For example: both are real. Each animal senses a different part of what is there. Nobody sees the whole flower.
items.why: This is an open question. Every animal has its own Umwelt, or sense-world. No animal senses everything.

items.p: What is 'the hard problem' that David Chalmers wrote about in 1995?
opts: How to make a hearing aid
Why signals in the brain feel like anything at all, like the taste of mango
items.why: Scientists can follow signals into the brain. But nobody yet knows why some signals feel like the colour yellow or the smell of rain. That is the hard problem, and it is still open.

items.p: Thomas Nagel asked, 'What is it like to be a bat?' Try to describe your bedroom the way a bat might sense it.
items.a: Any imaginative answer that uses echoes is good. For example: the walls give sharp, quick echoes. The bed gives a soft, slow echo. The open window gives no echo at all.
items.why: This is a way of imagining another animal's sense-world. Nagel's point is that we can imagine, but we may never truly know.

items.p: Draw the same mango three ways: as you see it, as a dog might smell it, and as a fly might taste it with its feet.
items.a: Any drawing that shows the mango in three different sense-worlds: colours for you, smell clouds for the dog, and taste spots under the fly's feet.
items.why: Each animal builds its own world from the signals its senses send. The mango is the same, but the worlds are different.
items.art: Three empty boxes side by side, each with a small mango outline in the middle.

experiments.title: Hold Your Nose: is flavour taste or smell?
experiments.question: Can you tell which spice is mixed into a spoon of sugar when your nose is pinched shut?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With your nose pinched, will you be able to name the spice in each spoon of sugar? Write yes or no next to each one, and say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the nose. Use the same amount of sugar each time, half a teaspoon, and the same small pinch of spice. The taster is blindfolded and tastes in a mixed-up order, so they cannot guess from the look or the order. They sip water between spoons. Each spoon is tasted twice: first with the nose pinched, then with the nose open.
results_table: What I guessed with my nose pinched
What I guessed with my nose open

materials.item: sugar, about 3 teaspoons
a pinch each of three ground spices from the kitchen: elaichi (cardamom), dalchini (cinnamon) and saunf (fennel)
4 small steel bowls or katoris, and 4 teaspoons
a dupatta or soft cloth, folded, to use as a blindfold
a glass of water
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Check for food allergies first. Use only a small pinch of spice, well mixed into the sugar, so nobody breathes in loose powder and coughs. The taster should keep the sugar on the tongue and not sniff the spoon.

schedule.what: Make four sugar bowls. Taste each one blindfolded, first with the nose pinched, then open. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then count: how many did you name with your nose pinched, and how many with it open?

flow.do: 1. Put half a teaspoon of sugar in each of the 4 katoris. 2. Leave bowl 1 plain. 3. Mix a small pinch of ground elaichi into bowl 2, dalchini into bowl 3 and saunf into bowl 4. 4. Stir each one well with its own spoon. 5. Write which bowl is which on a hidden piece of paper.
flow.say: We are going to find out how much of the taste of food comes from your tongue. And how much comes from your nose. Each bowl has sugar. Three of them have a secret spice too.
flow.kid: Put sugar in four bowls. Leave one plain. Mix a tiny pinch of spice into each of the others. Stir well. Hide the list of which is which.
flow.parent: Grind whole spices with a little sugar in a mortar if you have no ground spice. Mix really well, so there are no lumps of spice to feel.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hold Your Nose test. You find out whether you taste a spice with your tongue or with your nose.

flow.do: 1. Tie the blindfold on the taster. 2. Ask them to make their guesses before tasting anything.
flow.say: Before we start, guess. With your nose pinched shut, will you be able to name the spice? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put on the blindfold. Now guess. With your nose pinched, will you name the spice?

ask.q: Where do you think taste comes from?
good: From my tongue and my nose.

flow.do: 1. The taster pinches their nose firmly shut. 2. Put about a quarter teaspoon from one bowl on their tongue. Choose the bowls in a mixed-up order. 3. They keep the nose pinched and say what they taste. 4. Write their guess. 5. They sip water. 6. Do all four bowls.
flow.say: Keep your nose pinched tight, the whole time. What can you taste? Is there a spice? Which one?
flow.kid: Pinch your nose tight. Keep it pinched. Taste the sugar. Is there a spice? Which one?
flow.parent: Most children say 'just sweet' for every bowl. If they name a spice, check that the nose is fully closed. Grainy bits of spice can also give a clue, so mix more finely next time.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: 1. Give a spoonful from the first bowl again, with the nose pinched. 2. Halfway through, say 'Let go!' 3. The taster lets go of their nose while the sugar is still in their mouth. 4. Repeat for every bowl, and write the new guesses.
flow.say: Pinch again. Taste. Now, let go of your nose! What happened?
flow.kid: Pinch your nose and taste. Now let go! What happened? Does the spice appear?

ask.q: What changed when you let go of your nose?
good: I could tell it was elaichi.

check.q: With your nose pinched, the elaichi sugar tasted only sweet. When you let go, you could taste elaichi. Why?
options: Letting go made your tongue work better
The smell of elaichi could float up to your nose again
The sugar melted
The elaichi was hiding at the bottom of the spoon
check.why: Your tongue only tastes sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Elaichi's flavour is a smell. When you chew, its molecules float from the back of your mouth up into your nose. Pinching stops the air moving, so the smell cannot get there. Picking 'tongue works better' usually means thinking all taste comes from the tongue.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about where the spice flavour comes from? What did you notice that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I noticed. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the spice flavour comes from my nose, not my tongue. What I noticed: with my nose pinched, all four bowls tasted just sweet. When I let go, I could name the spice. Why: the smell of the spice floats up into my nose when I chew.

experiments.title: The Two-Point Test: where is touch sharpest?
experiments.question: Which parts of your skin can feel two points close together, and which feel them as just one?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put these in order, from the place you think feels most detail to the place that feels least: fingertip, palm, forearm, back. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the place on the skin. Use the same testers and press just as gently every time, so both points touch at the same moment. Mix in some touches with only one point, so the person cannot just say 'two' every time. Do 3 two-point touches at each gap on each place, with one single-point touch mixed in.

materials.item: 9 toothpicks
4 strips of thick cardboard, each about 8 cm long and 2 cm wide
a ruler from a school geometry box
sticky tape
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Touch gently. Use toothpicks with blunt ends, or snip the sharp tips off first. Never touch near the eyes or the face.

schedule.what: Make four testers with different gaps. Test the fingertip, palm, forearm and back. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw an outline of a body and colour the places that felt the most detail.

flow.do: 1. On each cardboard strip, mark two dots with the ruler. The gaps are 0.5 cm on the first strip and 1 cm on the second. They are 2 cm on the third and 4 cm on the fourth. 2. Poke a toothpick through each dot, blunt end sticking out about 1 cm on the same side. 3. Tape them firmly in place. 4. Keep one extra toothpick as the 'one point' tester.
flow.say: We're making four touch testers. Each has two toothpick points, with a different gap between them. We'll find out where your skin can tell two points from one.
flow.kid: Make four testers. Each has two toothpick points. The gaps are 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 centimetres. Check with a ruler.
flow.parent: A grown-up pokes the holes. Many toothpicks are pointed at both ends. If yours are, a grown-up snips the very tip off each point with scissors, so it presses without pricking. Both points must stick out the same amount, or one will touch first and give the answer away. Test each tester on your own palm first: both points should press together.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Point Test. You make tools to find out where your skin feels the most detail.

flow.do: 1. The person being tested shuts their eyes. 2. Start with the fingertip and the 0.5 cm tester. Touch it gently 3 times with the tester and once with the single toothpick, in a mixed-up order. 3. Ask 'one or two?' each time. 4. If they said two for at least 2 of the 3 two-point touches, write yes for that gap. 5. Do the same with the 1 cm, 2 cm and 4 cm testers. 6. Then test the palm, the forearm and the upper back in the same way.
flow.say: Eyes shut. I'm going to touch your skin. Sometimes with one point, sometimes with two. Each time, tell me: one or two?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Someone touches your skin with the points. Each time, say: one or two? Be honest. Guessing is fine.
flow.parent: What to expect: most fingertips feel two points even at 0.5 cm. The palm usually needs about 1 cm. The forearm often needs 4 cm or more. On the back, even 4 cm can feel like one point. If the results are mixed, do 2 more touches.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Look at the table together. Put the places in order, from the one that felt most detail to the one that felt least.
flow.say: Which place could feel two points closest together? Why would that part of your body need to feel so much detail?
flow.kid: Which place felt two points closest together? Why might your fingertips need that?

check.q: Your fingertip felt two points 0.5 cm apart. Your back felt two points 4 cm apart as just one. Why?
options: The skin on your back is thicker, so the points can't reach
Your fingertip has touch receptors packed much closer together
You pressed harder on the fingertip
Your back can't feel touch at all
check.why: On your fingertip, touch receptors are packed very close. So two points land on two different receptors. On your back, receptors are far apart. Two points 4 cm apart can land in the patch of just one receptor, so they feel like one. Picking 'thicker skin' is a good thought, but your back felt the touch clearly. It just could not tell one point from two.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about touch? What did you find that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I found. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: fingertips feel the most detail. What I found: my fingertip felt two points at 0.5 cm, but my back felt two points 4 cm apart as one. Why: fingertips have touch receptors packed closer together.

experiments.context: This is the Two-Point Test. You touch the skin with two toothpick points at different gaps, and find where the skin can tell two points from one.

experiments.title: Point at the Sound: are two ears better than one?
experiments.question: Can you point to where a sound comes from with your eyes shut? Do you need both ears to do it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Out of 8 sounds, how many will you point to correctly with two ears? How many with one ear blocked? Which direction will be hardest, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of ears. Use the same sound, at the same loudness, from the same 8 places, at the same distance of about 2 big steps. Do the places in a mixed-up order each time.
results_table: One ear blocked: right or wrong?

materials.item: two steel spoons, or a small bell
a dupatta or soft cloth, folded, to use as a blindfold
a stool or chair in a clear space in the middle of a room
a small ball of cotton wool, to block one ear
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Clear the floor so the blindfolded person cannot trip. Never make the sound right next to anyone's ear. Do not push the cotton wool deep into the ear: just hold it at the opening.

schedule.what: Make 8 sounds from around the room with two ears, then 8 with one ear blocked. Score each round.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Count the right answers for two ears and for one ear. Draw a bar for each.

flow.do: 1. Put the stool in the middle of a clear room. 2. The listener sits on it and puts on the blindfold. 3. Choose 8 places around them, about 2 big steps away: front, behind, left, right, front-left, front-right, back-left and back-right.
flow.say: You're going to be a sound detective. I'll click two spoons from somewhere in the room. Point to where you think the sound came from.
flow.kid: Sit on the stool. Put on the blindfold. Listen for a click. Point to where it came from.
flow.context: This is the first step of Point at the Sound. You find out whether you can point to a sound with your eyes shut, and whether two ears help.

flow.do: 1. Walk quietly to one of the 8 places. 2. Click the spoons once, softly. 3. The listener points. If they point within about an arm's width of you, it is right. 4. Write right or wrong. 5. Do all 8 places in a mixed-up order.
flow.say: Ready? Listen... Point! Now wait for the next one.
flow.kid: Listen. Point to the click. Wait for the next one. Keep your eyes covered.
flow.parent: Walk quietly in socks, so your footsteps do not give the answer away. Make each click the same, soft but clear.

flow.do: 1. The listener blocks one ear. They hold a small ball of cotton wool at the opening and press their flat palm firmly over that ear. 2. Do all 8 places again, in a new mixed-up order. 3. Write right or wrong for each.
flow.say: Now block one ear, tightly. Let's see if you can still find the sounds.
flow.kid: Block one ear. Press your palm over it, tight. Now point to the clicks again.
flow.parent: Blocking an ear by hand never stops all the sound, so the difference may be smaller than you expect. If the scores are the same, make the clicks much softer, or rub two fingers together instead. Sounds straight in front or behind are often mixed up, even with two ears.

flow.do: Count the right answers in each round and compare them.
flow.say: How many did you get with two ears? With one? Which places were hardest?
flow.kid: Count your right answers. Two ears or one: which was better? Which places were hardest?

check.q: In the sound test, most people find sounds better with two ears than with one. Why?
options: Two ears make every sound twice as loud
The brain compares when and how loudly the sound reaches each ear
One ear only hears high sounds
The blindfold blocks some of the sound
check.why: A sound on your left reaches your left ear a tiny bit sooner and a little louder. Your brain compares the two ears and works out the direction. With one ear blocked, it has much less to compare. Picking 'twice as loud' usually means thinking loudness is all that matters. But the difference between the ears is the real clue.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now about two ears? What did you find that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I found. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: two ears are better for finding sounds. What I found: I got 7 out of 8 right with two ears, but only 4 out of 8 with one ear blocked. Why: my brain compares my two ears to work out where the sound is.

experiments.context: This is Point at the Sound. Blindfolded, you point to clicks from around the room, first with two ears and then with one ear blocked.

activities.title: One Quiet Minute: what are your senses telling you?

materials.item: a phone or clock to time one minute
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Do this sitting down, somewhere safe.

schedule.what: Sit still for one minute with eyes shut, then list everything you noticed with each sense.

activities.record: Draw six columns: ears, skin, nose, tongue, eyes, and inside my body. Write everything you noticed in the right column.

flow.do: 1. Sit down together, somewhere ordinary, like the kitchen or the balcony. 2. Set a timer for one minute. 3. Both of you close your eyes.
flow.say: For one minute, let's be completely still and quiet, with our eyes shut. Notice everything your body is telling you. Every sound, every smell, every touch, and anything you feel inside you. Don't say anything until the timer rings.
flow.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. For one minute, just notice. Every sound. Every smell. Every touch.
flow.context: This is One Quiet Minute. It is a way to start noticing your senses, before learning how they work.

flow.do: When the timer rings, each of you makes a six-column list: ears, skin, nose, tongue, eyes, and inside my body.
flow.say: Now let's write everything we noticed. Put each thing under the sense that noticed it. Which column is longest?
flow.kid: Open your eyes. Make six columns: ears, skin, nose, tongue, eyes, and inside my body. Write everything you noticed.
flow.parent: Good finds: a fan humming, a bird outside, the floor pressing on your bottom, a cooking smell, the taste left from breakfast, warmth from the sun. For 'inside my body': feeling hungry or thirsty, a heartbeat, tired legs, needing the toilet. Children are often surprised how much they notice with their eyes shut.

flow.do: Compare your two lists, and talk about the questions.
flow.say: Did you notice anything you never usually notice? Was the fan there before we started, or did we just not hear it?
flow.kid: Compare lists. Did you notice something new? Was it there before, or did you just not notice it?
flow.think: What do you wonder about your senses? Write one question. You'll find many answers in this unit.

activities.context: This is a one-minute noticing activity. You sit still with your eyes shut and notice everything your senses tell you.

activities.title: Feel the Sound: three ways to feel and see a vibration

materials.item: a balloon, blown up and tied
a phone playing music with a strong beat
a bowl, cling film and a rubber band
a pinch of sugar or salt grains
a big steel plate or pan, and a steel ladle
a table and a pencil

activities.safety: Never bang the plate near anyone's ears. Keep the phone volume moderate, not at its loudest.

schedule.what: Feel music through a balloon, watch grains jump on a cling-film drum, and hear a tap through a table.

activities.record: Draw the path of a sound: from the plate, through the air, to the cling film. Then draw your ear doing the same.

flow.do: 1. Play music with a strong beat on the phone. 2. Hold the balloon between both hands, touching the phone's speaker. 3. Feel it. 4. Move it away slowly.
flow.say: Hold the balloon against the speaker. What do your hands feel? Sound is a vibration of the air. The balloon picks up the vibration, just like your eardrum does.
flow.kid: Hold the balloon against the speaker. Can you feel it shake? That shaking is sound.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel the Sound. You feel sound with your hands, to find out that sound is a vibration.

flow.do: 1. Stretch cling film tightly over the bowl, like a drum skin, and hold it with the rubber band. 2. Sprinkle a few sugar grains on top. 3. Hold the steel plate about one hand's length above the bowl, a little to one side. 4. Bang it hard with the ladle. 5. Watch the grains.
flow.say: This cling film is like your eardrum. Watch the sugar when I bang the plate.
flow.kid: Stretch cling film over a bowl. Sprinkle sugar on top. Bang a plate near it. Watch the sugar jump!
flow.parent: The cling film must be tight, like a drum. Hold the plate close, about one hand's length away. Sugar or salt grains jump best because they are light. If they hardly move, bang harder or hold the plate closer. A phone playing a deep bass note held just above the film also works.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts one ear flat on the table. 2. Tap the far end of the table gently with a pencil. 3. Then lift their head and tap again the same way.
flow.say: Put your ear on the table. I'll tap the other end. Now lift your head and listen again. Which was louder?
flow.kid: Put your ear on the table. Listen to the tap. Now lift your head. Which was louder?
flow.parent: Most children hear the tap much louder through the table. Sound travels well through solid things, because their particles are packed close.

flow.do: Talk about how all three were the same thing.
flow.say: The balloon, the cling film and the table all shook. Your eardrum shakes in the same way. Behind it, three tiny bones pass the shaking to your cochlea.
flow.kid: The balloon, the film and the table all shook. Your eardrum shakes just like that.

check.q: The sugar jumped on the cling film when the plate was banged. What reached the cling film?
options: Shaking air, a vibration
Tiny bits of steel from the plate
Light from the plate
Nothing, the sugar jumped by itself
check.why: The plate shook, and made the air around it shake. The shaking travelled through the air and shook the cling film, just as sound shakes your eardrum. Picking 'bits of steel' usually means thinking sound is a thing that flies across. Really, only the shaking moves across. The air itself only moves back and forth a tiny bit.

activities.context: This is Feel the Sound. You feel and see sound shaking things, using a balloon, a cling-film drum and a table.

activities.title: The Mystery Bag: how much can fingertips tell?

materials.item: a cloth bag or a pillowcase
8 small things: a coin, a key, an elaichi pod, a rubber band, a cotton ball, a steel spoon, a dry rajma bean and a button
a pair of thick socks, to wear on the hands

activities.safety: Nothing sharp in the bag. Small things are a choking risk for babies, so keep them away from little brothers and sisters.

schedule.what: Name things in a bag by touch, first with bare fingers, then with socks on your hands.

activities.record: Write two numbers: how many things you named with bare fingers, and how many with socks on.

flow.do: Put the 8 things in the bag without your child seeing them.
flow.say: There are 8 things hidden in this bag. You can only use your fingers. Before you guess, describe each one: is it rough or smooth, hard or soft, cold or warm, heavy or light?
flow.kid: There are 8 things in the bag. Feel them without looking. Describe each one before you guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Mystery Bag. You name hidden things by touch alone.

flow.do: 1. Your child reaches in with bare hands. 2. For each thing, they describe it first, then guess. 3. Count the right guesses.
flow.say: Tell me how it feels first. Then guess. Which part of your hand are you using most?
flow.kid: Feel one thing. Say how it feels. Then guess what it is.

ask.q: How did you tell the coin from the button?
good: The coin was cold and heavy.
The coin had a ridged edge. The button had holes.

flow.do: 1. Mix the things up. 2. Your child puts thick socks over both hands. 3. They try again. 4. Count the right guesses.
flow.say: Now put socks on your hands, and try again. Is it easier or harder? Why?
flow.kid: Put socks on your hands. Try again. Is it harder? Why?
flow.parent: With socks on, most children can still tell big shapes, but lose small details like the ridges on a coin or the seam of an elaichi pod. The sock stops the tiny pushes from reaching the touch receptors in the fingertips.

flow.do: Talk about the star-nosed mole and Braille.
flow.say: A star-nosed mole finds food in dark tunnels with 22 fleshy fingers on its nose. Blind people read Braille with their fingertips. Why fingertips, and not elbows?
flow.kid: A star-nosed mole touches with its nose. Blind people read with their fingertips. Why not elbows?
flow.think: Cold steel feels colder than a cotton ball, even in the same room. Are they really different temperatures?

activities.context: This is the Mystery Bag. You name hidden things using touch alone, first with bare fingers and then with socks on your hands.

activities.title: The Fading Coin: senses notice changes

materials.item: a coin
a small jar with a few crushed elaichi pods or a little coffee
a clock or phone with seconds

activities.safety: Waft the smell towards your nose. Do not put your nose right into the jar.

schedule.what: Feel a coin on your skin fade away, and score a smell as it fades.

activities.record: Write how many seconds until you stopped feeling the coin. Then write your smell scores, from 5 down.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies or sits still with their forearm resting on a table, palm up, eyes shut. 2. Put the coin gently on the forearm and start the clock. 3. They raise a finger of the other hand when they can no longer feel the coin. 4. Write the time. 5. Then nudge the coin slightly. Ask what happened.
flow.say: Keep very still. Raise a finger when you stop feeling the coin. Now... I'll move it a tiny bit.
flow.kid: Eyes shut. Keep still. Raise a finger when you stop feeling the coin.
flow.parent: Many children stop noticing the coin within about half a minute if they keep perfectly still. When you nudge it, they feel it again at once. Touch receptors mostly report changes. If they still feel it after a minute, that's fine: everyone is different.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fading Coin. You find out what happens when a touch stays exactly the same.

flow.do: 1. Your child wafts the smell from the jar towards their nose and gives it a score from 5 (very strong) to 0 (nothing). 2. Keep wafting gently every 15 seconds for 2 minutes, and score each time. 3. Then go into another room for 2 minutes, come back and smell again.
flow.say: Score the smell from 5 to 0. Keep going every 15 seconds. Does it stay the same?
flow.kid: Waft the smell. Score it: 5 is very strong, 0 is nothing. Again every 15 seconds.
flow.parent: The score usually drops a little, perhaps from 5 to 3. After a break, it often jumps back up. This is called adaptation. It is why you cannot smell your own home, but visitors can.

flow.do: Talk about why senses work like this.
flow.say: Your senses mostly tell you what is changing. Why might that be useful?
flow.kid: Your senses mostly notice changes. Why might that be useful?

check.q: You stopped feeling the coin, but felt it again when it moved. What does that show?
options: The coin got lighter
Touch receptors mostly report changes, not things that stay the same
Your skin went to sleep for ever
The coin fell off
check.why: Many touch receptors send lots of signals when something starts or moves, and then go quiet if nothing changes. So a still coin fades. A tiny nudge is a change, and they fire again. Picking 'skin went to sleep' is close, but your skin felt the nudge straight away, so it was still working.

activities.context: This is the Fading Coin. You find out that your senses stop noticing things that stay the same, using a coin on your skin and a smell in a jar.

activities.title: The Blue Mango: make your cones tired

materials.item: white paper, 2 sheets
bright sketch pens or crayons: blue, pink and black
a clock or phone with seconds

activities.safety: Never stare at the Sun or a bright bulb. Only stare at the paper drawing.

schedule.what: Draw a blue mango with a pink leaf, stare at it for 30 seconds, then look at white paper.

activities.record: Draw what you saw on the white paper, in the colours you saw.

flow.do: 1. On one sheet, draw a big mango shape, as big as your hand. 2. Colour it in solid, bright blue. 3. Draw a leaf on top and colour it pink. 4. Put a small black dot in the middle of the mango.
flow.say: We're drawing a strange mango: a blue mango with a pink leaf. Colour it in thickly, with no white gaps.
flow.kid: Draw a big mango. Colour it bright blue. Give it a pink leaf. Put a black dot in the middle.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blue Mango. You draw a mango in the wrong colours, to trick the colour cells in your eyes.

flow.do: 1. Put the drawing in good light. 2. Your child stares at the black dot for 30 seconds without moving their eyes. 3. Then they look straight at the blank white sheet. 4. Wait a few seconds.
flow.say: Stare at the black dot. Don't move your eyes. Count 30 slow seconds with me. Now look at the white paper. What do you see?
flow.kid: Stare at the dot for 30 seconds. Don't move your eyes! Now look at the white paper. What do you see?
flow.parent: Most children see a faint yellow-orange mango with a green leaf floating on the white paper. It lasts a few seconds. If nothing appears, colour more thickly, use brighter light, and stare a full 30 seconds without blinking much.

flow.do: Explain what happened, using the cones.
flow.say: Your eye has cones for three colours. Staring at blue tired out your blue cones. When you looked at white, the tired blue cones sent weaker signals than the others. So your brain saw the colour opposite to blue, which is yellow. Pink light works your red and blue cones but hardly your green ones. So after the pink leaf, your green cones sent the strongest signals, and you saw a green leaf.
flow.kid: Staring tired out some of your colour cells. Then the rested ones sent stronger signals. So you saw the opposite colours!

check.q: After staring at the blue mango, you saw a yellow mango on white paper. Why?
options: The paper had a yellow mango on it all along
Your blue cones were tired, so the others sent more signals
Blue paint got into your eye
The light in the room changed colour
check.why: Cones get tired when they work hard for a long time. White paper sends light to all your cones. The tired blue cones answered weakly, so your brain got more signals from the others, and saw yellow. Picking 'the paper had a yellow mango' shows how real an afterimage feels. But the paper was blank. The colour was made in your eye and brain.

flow.do: Talk about where the yellow mango was.
flow.say: The paper was blank. So where was the yellow mango? On the paper, in your eye, or in your brain?
flow.kid: The paper was blank. So where was the yellow mango?
flow.think: If your eyes and brain can make a colour that is not there, how do you know the colours you usually see are there?

activities.context: This is the Blue Mango. You stare at a mango drawn in the wrong colours, then see it in the right colours on a blank page. It shows how your eye's colour cells get tired.

activities.title: Two Eyes, One Picture: the pencil-tip test

materials.item: two pencils with caps, or two pens with the caps on

activities.safety: Use capped pens or blunt pencils. Keep them at arm's length from your face.

schedule.what: Try to touch two pencil tips together with both eyes open, then with one eye shut.

activities.record: Write how many touches out of 5 you managed with two eyes, and with one eye.

flow.do: 1. Hold a pencil upright at arm's length. 2. Your child holds another pencil and tries to touch its tip to the tip of yours, coming from the side. 3. Do it 5 times with both eyes open. 4. Count the hits.
flow.say: Touch your pencil tip to mine. Come in from the side. Let's try 5 times.
flow.kid: Touch your pencil tip to the other pencil tip. Try 5 times. Count your hits.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Eyes, One Picture. You find out why we have two eyes, using two pencils.

flow.do: 1. Move your pencil to a new spot. 2. Your child closes one eye. 3. They try 5 times again. 4. Count the hits.
flow.say: Now close one eye, and try again. Is it easier or harder?
flow.kid: Close one eye. Try 5 more times. Easier or harder?
flow.parent: Most children miss much more often with one eye shut. They overshoot or stop short. Each eye sees from a slightly different place, and the brain compares the two pictures to judge how far away things are.

flow.do: Show the 'jumping thumb' to see the two pictures.
flow.say: Hold your thumb up in front of you. Close one eye, then the other, again and again. Your thumb jumps! Each eye sees a slightly different picture. Your brain joins them and works out how far away things are.
flow.kid: Hold up your thumb. Close one eye, then the other. Your thumb jumps! Each eye sees it from a different place.
flow.think: An owl has both eyes on the front of its face. A pigeon has eyes on the sides. Which one sees further around? Which one judges distance better?

activities.context: This is Two Eyes, One Picture. You try to touch two pencil tips together, first with both eyes open and then with one shut.

activities.title: Senses You Forgot You Had: balance, body position, warm and cold

materials.item: 3 steel bowls, each big enough to put a hand in
cold water from the fridge, or tap water with a few ice cubes
warm water: a grown-up mixes a little hot water from a kettle or geyser into cold water
a towel
a clock or phone with seconds

activities.safety: Do the balance test next to a wall on a clear floor, with a grown-up standing close. The warm water must be only comfortably warm, like a bath. A grown-up tests it with an elbow first.

schedule.what: Stand on one foot with eyes open and shut, touch your nose with your eyes shut, and feel warm and cold water fool your hands.

activities.record: Write how many seconds you stood on one foot with eyes open and with eyes shut. Write how many times out of 6 you touched your nose. Write what each hand felt in the middle bowl.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands next to a wall, on one foot, with eyes open. 2. Count the seconds until the other foot touches the floor. Stop at 30. 3. Now they try again with eyes shut. 4. Write both times.
flow.say: Stand on one foot and look straight ahead. I'll count. Now do it again with your eyes shut. Before you try, guess: will it be easier or harder? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand on one foot near a wall. Count how long you can stay up. Now close your eyes and try again. Is it harder?
flow.parent: Most children stand for the full 30 seconds with eyes open, but only a few seconds with eyes shut. The brain balances with three senses together: the eyes, the balance organs in the inner ears and the stretch sensors in the muscles. Shutting the eyes takes one away.
flow.context: This is the first step of Senses You Forgot You Had. You test your balance sense, one of the many senses that is not on the list of five.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes and stretches both arms out to the sides. 2. They touch the tip of their nose with one pointing finger, then put the arm back out. 3. Do it 3 times with each hand. 4. Count the touches out of 6.
flow.say: Eyes shut. Arms out wide. Now touch the tip of your nose with one finger. How did your finger know where your nose was?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Stretch your arms out. Touch your nose with one finger. Now the other hand. How did you know where your nose was?

ask.q: How did your finger find your nose without your eyes?
good: My body knows where my arm is.
Something in my arm told my brain where it was.

flow.parent: Most children touch their nose almost every time. Stretch sensors in the muscles and joints tell the brain where each part of the body is. This sense is called proprioception.

flow.do: 1. Fill three bowls: cold water on the left, water straight from the tap in the middle, warm water on the right. 2. A grown-up tests the warm bowl with an elbow. 3. Your child puts the left hand in the cold bowl and the right hand in the warm bowl. 4. They hold them there for 1 minute. 5. Then both hands go into the middle bowl at the same time.
flow.say: Before you put both hands in the middle bowl, guess: will they feel the same? Now try it. What does each hand tell you?
flow.kid: Left hand in the cold bowl. Right hand in the warm bowl. Wait one minute. Now put both hands in the middle bowl. What does each hand feel?
flow.parent: The hand that was in cold water feels the middle bowl as warm. The hand that was in warm water feels it as cold. The warm and cold nerve endings report the change from what they are used to, not the exact temperature. The English thinker John Locke wrote about this test in 1690.

check.q: Both your hands were in the same middle bowl. The hand from the cold bowl felt warm, and the hand from the warm bowl felt cold. Why?
options: The middle bowl was warm on one side and cold on the other
Your warm and cold nerve endings report the change from what they were used to
One of your hands was broken
Water changes temperature when you touch it
check.why: Both hands were in exactly the same water. The hand that had been in cold water felt a change towards warmer, so it reported warm. The other hand felt a change towards colder. Picking 'warm on one side' is a natural guess, but you can swap hands and the feeling swaps too.

flow.do: Dry hands with the towel. Then talk about the senses inside the body.
flow.say: Close your eyes for a moment. Are you hungry? Thirsty? Do you need the toilet? Which sense told you? None of your eyes, ears, nose, tongue or skin did.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Are you hungry or thirsty? Which part of you told you?
flow.parent: This is interoception, sensing the inside of the body. Stretch sensors notice a full stomach or bladder. Cells in the brain notice when the blood is too salty, and that makes you thirsty.
flow.think: Aristotle counted five senses. How many have you used today?

activities.context: This is Senses You Forgot You Had. You test three senses that are not on the usual list of five: balance, knowing where your body is, and feeling warm and cold.

projects.title: Train Your Nose: can smelling get better with practice?

materials.item: 6 small jars or covered katoris
6 smelly things from the kitchen: jeera, laung, a slice of ginger, curry leaves, a little coffee and a strip of lemon peel
masking tape and a pen, to number the jars
a dupatta or soft cloth, folded, to use as a blindfold
a notebook for the smell diary

projects.safety: Waft each smell towards your nose. Never sniff spices hard, or put your nose into the jar. Put in a fresh slice of ginger and fresh lemon peel each day, because they dry out. Throw out anything that goes mouldy.

schedule.what: Make 6 numbered smell jars. Test yourself blindfolded and write your first score. Then practise once with your eyes open, saying each name.
Practise with your eyes open: smell each jar, say its name and one word for what it smells like.
Practise again. Then test a family member who has not practised.
Test yourself blindfolded again, in a new order. Compare your day 1 and day 4 scores. Make a bar chart.

projects.record: Write your score out of 6 on day 1 and on day 4. Draw two bars. Write one sentence about what changed.

flow.do: 1. Put a little of each smelly thing in its own jar. 2. Number the jars 1 to 6 on tape underneath, so the number cannot be seen from above. 3. Write which number is which in the notebook, and hide it.
flow.say: We're going to find out if noses can learn. Doctors use smell training to help people whose sense of smell has gone weak, for example after an illness.
flow.kid: Put each smelly thing in a jar. Number the jars underneath. Write the list and hide it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Train Your Nose. It is a four-day project to find out if practice makes smelling better.

flow.do: 1. Blindfold your child. 2. Give the jars in a mixed-up order. 3. They waft each one and name it. 4. Write their first score out of 6. 5. Then take off the blindfold and go through them once, saying each name.
flow.say: Wave the air towards your nose. What is it? It's fine not to know. Lots of people know a smell but can't find its name.
flow.kid: Blindfold on. Waft each jar towards your nose. Name it. It's fine if you can't.
flow.parent: A first score of 2 or 3 out of 6 is very normal. People often say 'I know it, but I can't think of the word'. Scientists call this the 'tip of the nose' feeling.

flow.do: On day 2 and day 3, go through all 6 jars with eyes open. Smell each one, say its name and choose one describing word for it, like 'warm', 'sharp' or 'sweet'.
flow.say: Smell it, say its name, and give it a describing word. Words help your brain hold on to a smell.
flow.kid: Smell each jar. Say its name. Give it one describing word, like warm or sharp.
flow.wait: Practise once a day for 2 days.
flow.parent: The Jahai people of the Malaysian rainforest have many words just for smells. A scientist called Asifa Majid found they name smells as easily as English speakers name colours.

flow.do: 1. On day 3, test a family member who has not practised. 2. On day 4, blindfold your child and test them again, in a new order. 3. Compare the scores.
flow.say: Let's see if your nose has learned. Did your score change from day 1?
flow.kid: Test a grown-up who hasn't practised. Then test yourself again. Did your score go up?

check.q: Your nose-test score went from 3 on day 1 to 6 on day 4. What is the best explanation?
options: Your nose grew bigger
Your brain got better at matching smells to their names
The spices got stronger
It was just luck, so practice never helps
check.why: Your nose is the same size. Your smell receptors detect molecules just as before. What changed is your brain. It learned to match each pattern of signals to a name. Picking 'just luck' is a good scientist's worry. That is why you also tested someone who had not practised, to compare.

flow.do: Make the bar chart. Then ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. Can noses learn? What did you find that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw two bars: day 1 and day 4. Then say what you think, what you found, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: practice makes me better at naming smells. What I found: I got 3 out of 6 on day 1 and 6 out of 6 on day 4. Papa, who did not practise, got 3. Why: my brain learned to link each smell to its name.

projects.context: This is Train Your Nose. Over four days you make six smell jars, test yourself, practise, and test again to see if your nose gets better.

challenges.title: Hear a Whisper Across the Room
challenges.problem: Someone whispers a word at the far side of a room. Build something that helps you hear the whisper from further away than your bare ears can.
constraints: You can only use things from home.
The whisperer must whisper the same way every time.
Measure, in footsteps, the furthest distance where you can still hear the word clearly.
materials: a plastic funnel and a piece of plastic pipe or a rubber tube, if you have them
general: Roll paper into a big cone, like an old ear trumpet. Hold the small end near your ear, not inside it, and point the wide end at the whisperer.
Cup your hands behind your ears to make bigger ear flaps.
Make the room quiet: switch off the fan and close the window.
creative: Join a funnel to a tube, like a doctor's stethoscope. Can you hear your own heartbeat with it?
Make two cones, one for each ear, so your brain can still compare the two sides.
Try a big ear flap shape copied from an animal: a fennec fox, an elephant or a bat.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own hearing helper. Draw it, build it and test it. How many footsteps further can you hear the whisper?

flow.do: 1. Stand facing the whisperer, close together. 2. Step backwards one footstep at a time while they whisper a word each time. 3. Stop when you can no longer hear the word clearly. 4. Count the footsteps.
flow.say: First, let's measure how far your bare ears can hear a whisper.
flow.kid: Step back one footstep at a time. Stop when you can't hear the whisper. Count your steps.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hear a Whisper Across the Room. First you measure how far away you can hear a whisper with bare ears.
flow.parent: In a small flat you may run out of room before the whisper fades. Then whisper more softly, or use a passage, or two rooms with the door open.

flow.do: List three ideas together before building anything.
flow.say: Before we build, let's think like engineers. Your ear flap collects sound and funnels it in. How could we make a bigger collector?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas for collecting more sound.
flow.parent: If ideas are slow to come, point at the ear flap. It collects sound. A bigger collector gathers more of the vibrating air.

flow.do: 1. Build each idea. 2. Test each one the same way as the bare-ear test. 3. Write the number of footsteps for each.
flow.say: Test each idea the same way. Same whisperer, same kind of word, same footsteps.
flow.kid: Build your ideas. Test each one the same way. Count the footsteps.
flow.parent: A big paper cone usually adds a few footsteps. Never put anything inside the ear canal. Hold the small end of the cone just at the opening.

check.q: Why does a big paper cone help you hear a whisper from further away?
options: It makes the whisper louder at the whisperer's mouth
It collects more of the vibrating air and funnels it into your ear
It blocks your other ear
Paper makes its own sound
check.why: Your ear flap collects sound. A big cone is a much bigger collector. It gathers vibrating air from a wider area and funnels it to your eardrum. Picking 'louder at the mouth' mixes up the two ends. The whisper is the same. You just collect more of it.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Here is what people usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something better?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ideas and the creative ideas. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Before electric hearing aids, people used big ear trumpets. Why do you think hearing aids became so small?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a hearing helper from paper and things at home, and measure how much further away you can hear a whisper.

challenges.title: A Kitchen Shelf for Someone Who Cannot See
challenges.problem: Imagine a friend who is blind is coming to cook with you. Six jars look exactly the same: sugar, salt, haldi, chilli powder, jeera and rice. Make labels they can read without seeing, so they can find the sugar first time.
constraints: The labels must work by touch or smell, not sight.
Nobody may open the jars to taste or sniff inside.
Test it: a blindfolded family member must find three things you call out.
materials: 6 jars or steel dabbas that look the same
rubber bands, string, buttons, felt, sandpaper or cardboard
glue, or a glue gun if you have one, used only by a grown-up
general: Put a different number of rubber bands around each jar: one for sugar, two for salt, and so on.
Stick a different texture on each lid: smooth cloth, rough sandpaper, a button, a ridge of string.
Make raised-dot labels, like Braille, with drops of glue that dry hard.
creative: Find a Braille alphabet in a book or online. Make the dots for the first letter of each jar, for example H for haldi and J for jeera.
Use shape as well as texture: a triangle of card for chilli, because chilli is sharp and hot.
Ask a blind person, or an organisation that works with blind people, what labels they really use.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own labelling system. Draw it, make it and test it with a blindfolded family member. Did they find all three things first time?

flow.do: 1. Line up the six jars. 2. Blindfold a family member. 3. Ask them to find the sugar without opening any jar. 4. See what happens.
flow.say: First, let's see how hard it is now. Can you find the sugar without seeing and without opening the jars?
flow.kid: Blindfold a grown-up. Ask them to find the sugar. They can't open the jars. Can they do it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the kitchen shelf challenge. First you find out how hard it is to find things on a shelf without seeing.

flow.do: Plan a labelling system together on paper.
flow.say: Your fingertips feel the most detail. How could we make each jar feel different?
flow.kid: Plan your labels. How can each jar feel different? Remember the Mystery Bag and the Two-Point Test.
flow.parent: Remind your child that fingertips can feel dots 0.5 cm apart. Braille dots are only about 2.5 millimetres apart.

flow.do: 1. Make the labels and stick them on. 2. Let any glue dry fully. 3. A grown-up uses the glue gun if you use one.
flow.say: Let's build it. Make each label as different to the touch as you can.
flow.kid: Make your labels. Stick them on. Ask a grown-up to use the glue gun.

flow.do: 1. Explain the system to a blindfolded family member. 2. Call out three things to find. 3. Count how many they find first time. 4. Improve the design.
flow.say: Now the test. Find the salt. Find the jeera. Find the sugar.
flow.kid: Tell a blindfolded grown-up your system. Call out three jars. Did they find them first time?

check.q: Which label is easiest to read by touch alone?
options: A label written in small blue letters
Three rubber bands round the jar
A label with a picture of salt
A shiny sticker
check.why: Rubber bands can be counted with your fingertips. Small blue letters, pictures and shiny stickers all feel flat and smooth, so they need eyes. Picking the picture usually means forgetting that the person cannot see it.

flow.think: Louis Braille invented his raised-dot writing at about 15 years old. What could you invent that would help someone?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make labels for six kitchen jars that a blind person can read by touch, then test them with a blindfolded family member.

opts: A way the body detects something from the world and sends a message to the brain
quiz.why: A sense detects something, like light or sound, and turns it into signals for the brain. Picking 'a feeling' mixes up sensing with emotions.

quiz.p: What does every sense send to the brain?
quiz.why: Light and sound never reach the brain. Only electric signals do. Picking 'real light or sound' is the most common idea, and it is not right.

quiz.p: Which part of the ear shakes first when sound reaches it?
quiz.why: Sound goes down the ear canal and shakes the eardrum first. Then three tiny bones pass the shaking to the cochlea. Picking the cochlea skips two steps.

quiz.p: Why do two ears help you find where a sound comes from?
opts: Two ears hear twice as much
The brain compares which ear the sound reaches first and loudest
One ear is for loud sounds and one for soft
quiz.why: A sound from one side reaches the nearer ear sooner and louder. The brain compares them. Picking 'twice as much' means thinking loudness is the only clue.

quiz.p: Why should you keep earphones at a low volume?
opts: Loud sound can break hair cells, and they do not grow back
Loud sound is only bad for grown-ups
quiz.why: In people, broken hair cells do not grow back, so the hearing loss lasts. Picking 'only bad for grown-ups' is wrong. Children's hair cells can break too.

quiz.p: Where on your body is touch sharpest?
quiz.why: Fingertips have touch receptors packed very close together. Picking 'the same everywhere' usually means not yet having tried the two-point test.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT one of the five basic tastes?
quiz.why: Chilli 'heat' is detected by nerve endings that warn of burning, not by taste buds. Picking umami is common, because it is the least known of the five tastes.

quiz.p: Can the back of your tongue taste sweet?
opts: No, only the tip tastes sweet
Yes, every part with taste buds tastes every taste
quiz.why: The tongue map is wrong. Taste receptors for every taste are spread across the tongue. Picking 'only the tip' is the old tongue map.

quiz.p: With your nose pinched, elaichi sugar tastes only sweet. Why?
opts: Elaichi's flavour is a smell, and pinching stops it reaching your nose
quiz.why: Most flavour is smell. The elaichi molecules float from your mouth into your nose, unless your nose is pinched. Picking 'tongue numb' is wrong, because you still tasted the sweetness.
Smell receptors are in a small patch high inside your nose. Picking 'tongue' mixes up smell and taste, which is easy, because they work together.

quiz.p: Which cells in your eye work in dim light but see no colour?
quiz.why: Rods work in dim light. That is why at night you see shapes but little colour. Cones see colour in brighter light.

quiz.p: Which animal can see ultraviolet stripes on flowers that we cannot see?
quiz.why: Honeybees see ultraviolet. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that guide bees to the nectar. Dogs and cats cannot see ultraviolet the way bees do.

quiz.p: How do bats find moths in the dark?
opts: By squeaking and listening for echoes
quiz.why: Bats use echolocation. They squeak and hear the echoes bounce back from moths. Some blind people use tongue clicks in the same way.

quiz.p: Which question do scientists still NOT know the answer to?
opts: Why do signals in the brain feel like the taste of mango or the colour red?
quiz.why: Scientists know a lot about how senses send signals. But how signals become experience is still a mystery. Some call it the hard problem.

quiz.p: How many senses do people have?
opts: Many more than five, such as balance, body position, warmth and cold, and thirst
quiz.why: Five is an old count, from Aristotle more than 2,300 years ago. Scientists count many more, each with its own receptors, though they do not agree on the exact number. Picking 'exactly five' is the answer many school books still give.

quiz.p: You stand on one foot with your eyes shut. Which sense helps you most to stay up?
opts: The balance sense in your inner ears
quiz.why: Your inner ears hold balance organs that sense gravity and the turning of your head. Picking 'hearing' is close, because the balance organs sit right next to the cochlea. But they do a different job.

applications: Hearing aids and cochlear implants. A cochlear implant sends electric signals straight to the nerve of the cochlea, so some deaf people can hear.
Ear protection for people who work with loud machines, and safe-volume settings on phones.
Braille books, Braille signs in lifts and on medicine boxes, and raised dots on Indian currency notes for people who cannot see well.
Tactile paving: the yellow ridged tiles on Metro platforms and footpaths that blind people can feel with their feet or a cane.
Eye tests and spectacles. The eye doctor checks how sharply each eye sees.
Cataract surgery, which gives sight back to millions of people. Aravind Eye Hospital in Madurai has done millions of these operations.
Gas companies add a strong-smelling chemical to cooking gas, which has no smell of its own, so people notice a leak.
Sniffer dogs at airports and in rescue work, finding people buried after earthquakes.
Food scientists design flavour, crunch and colour together, because the senses mix.
Phones that buzz in your hand, using the touch receptors that feel vibration.
Night-vision cameras and heat cameras let people sense infrared, which our eyes cannot.
Smell training is used by doctors to help people whose sense of smell has gone weak after an illness.

open_questions.q: How do electric signals in the brain become experiences, like the colour of a mango or the smell of rain?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can follow the signals into the brain, but nobody knows why they feel like anything at all. This is sometimes called the hard problem.

open_questions.q: Is the red you see the same as the red your friend sees?
open_questions.why_open: You both call it red and point at the same things. But there is no way, so far, to compare the experiences themselves.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a bat, or a bee, or a fish?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what their senses detect, but not what it feels like to them.

open_questions.q: How many smells can people tell apart?
open_questions.why_open: One team estimated at least a trillion. Others showed that the answer depends on the maths used. Nobody can test every mixture.

open_questions.q: Why can birds grow new hair cells in their ears, but people cannot?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are studying the genes that switch this on in birds, hoping one day to help people with hearing loss.

open_questions.q: Is there a sixth basic taste, such as fat?
open_questions.why_open: Some tests suggest people can taste fat on its own. Scientists are still arguing about whether it counts as a basic taste.

open_questions.q: How exactly does the brain join all the senses into one world, at the same moment?
open_questions.why_open: Each sense is handled in different parts of the brain, at slightly different speeds. How they are bound together into one experience is still not understood.

open_questions.q: Do insects and other small animals feel what they sense?
open_questions.why_open: Flies and bees learn, remember and avoid harm. Whether they have any inner experience is still argued about.

ask_kids: Close your eyes for ten seconds. What can you hear right now that you didn't notice before?
What does this food taste like if you hold your nose?
Which of your senses woke up first this morning?
Can you smell our house? Why can visitors smell it better than we can?
If you could borrow one animal's sense for a day, which would it be?
Where is the sound of that horn coming from? How do you know without looking?
Is your shirt touching you right now? Did you feel it before I asked?
Why does chilli feel hot, even when it's cold?
What smell brings back a happy memory for you?
How would you find your way to the kitchen in the dark?
Is this chutney as bitter for you as it is for me? How could we find out?
Are you thirsty right now? Which sense tells you?

jokes.j: Why did the nose go to school?
jokes.a: It wanted to be a little more scent-sible.

jokes.j: What did one ear say to the other ear?
jokes.a: Between us, we have a brain.

jokes.j: Why don't noses ever get bored?
jokes.a: There's always something in the air.

jokes.j: Why did the tongue get top marks?
jokes.a: It had good taste.

jokes.j: What do you call a deer with no eyes?
jokes.a: No idea.

jokes.j: Why was the eye doctor so calm?
jokes.a: She always looked on the bright side.

jokes.j: Why did the bat need a hearing aid?
jokes.a: It kept missing the echo.

jokes.j: What did the chilli say to the mint?
jokes.a: You're so cool. I'm just hot-headed.

jokes.j: Why did the fly walk all over the mango?
jokes.a: It wanted a taste, and its feet were its tongue.

jokes.j: Why did the coin stop talking to the arm?
jokes.a: It felt it was being ignored.

jokes.j: What did the eardrum say to the loud music?
jokes.a: Please, don't beat me up.

jokes.j: Why are fingertips so good at reading?
jokes.a: They always get the point. Sometimes two.

jokes.j: What do you call a sense that tells jokes?
jokes.a: A sense of humour.

jokes.j: Why did the cat refuse the laddoo?
jokes.a: It couldn't taste the sweet side of life.

jokes.j: Why do noses run?
jokes.a: Because they can't walk.

jokes.j: Why did the blue mango turn yellow?
jokes.a: Your cones got tired of looking at it.

jokes.j: What did the bee say to the flower?
jokes.a: I can see your secret stripes.

jokes.j: Why was the cochlea so good at music?
jokes.a: It had thousands of tiny hairs, all perfectly in tune.

jokes.j: Why did the parrot laugh at the chilli?
jokes.a: It didn't feel the burn.

maths.problem: In the Two-Point Test, a child felt two points on her fingertip when they were 0.5 cm apart. On her forearm, the points had to be 4 cm apart. How many times bigger was the forearm gap?
maths.explain: The forearm gap was 4 cm. The fingertip gap was 0.5 cm, which is half a centimetre. Two half centimetres make 1 cm, so 4 cm holds 4 × 2 = 8 half centimetres. So the forearm gap was 8 times bigger. The fingertip feels detail 8 times finer.
maths.context: This is about the Two-Point Test. You touch the skin with two toothpick points and find the smallest gap where they still feel like two.

chart.title: Smallest gap felt as two points

maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'fingertips feel more'. They ask 'how much more?' Dividing one gap by the other tells us.

maths.problem: In Point at the Sound, a child found 7 out of 8 sounds with two ears, and 4 out of 8 with one ear blocked. Draw a bar for each. How many more did she find with two ears?
maths.answer: 3 more sounds. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw two bars, one 7 tall and one 4 tall. The difference between them is 7 − 4 = 3. So she found 3 more sounds with two ears.
maths.context: This is about Point at the Sound. Blindfolded, you point to clicks from 8 places around the room, first with two ears and then with one ear blocked.
maths.why_maths: Two numbers in a table are easy to miss. Two bars side by side show the difference at a glance.

maths.problem: In the Hold Your Nose test, a family of 4 people each tasted 3 spiced sugars with their noses pinched. Make a tally of how many spices were named correctly: Amma 0, Papa 1, Didi 0, me 0. Then, with noses open: Amma 3, Papa 3, Didi 2, me 3. How many were named correctly in all, with noses pinched and with noses open?
maths.answer: With noses pinched: 1 out of 12. With noses open: 11 out of 12.
maths.explain: With noses pinched, add 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 1. With noses open, add 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 11. Each person tasted 3 spices, and there were 4 people, so there were 4 × 3 = 12 tastes in each round. So 1 out of 12 pinched, and 11 out of 12 open.
maths.context: This is about the Hold Your Nose test. You taste spoons of sugar with secret spices, first with your nose pinched shut, then with it open.
maths.why_maths: One person's result could be a fluke. Adding up the whole family's results shows whether the pattern is real.

maths.problem: In the Fading Coin activity, a child stopped feeling the coin after 25 seconds the first time, 20 seconds the second time and 30 seconds the third time. Put the times in order. What is the middle value?
maths.answer: In order: 20, 25, 30 seconds. The middle value is 25 seconds.
maths.explain: Put the three times in order from smallest to biggest: 20, 25, 30. The middle one is 25. So the coin usually faded after about 25 seconds.
maths.context: This is about the Fading Coin. You put a coin on a still arm and time how long until you stop feeling it.
maths.why_maths: Times are never exactly the same twice. The middle value is a fair way to say what usually happens.

maths.problem: In the Blue Mango activity, you stare at the dot for 30 seconds. The yellow afterimage lasted 8 seconds. Then you tried staring for 60 seconds, and it lasted 15 seconds. About how many times longer did you stare the second time? Did the afterimage last longer too?
maths.answer: You stared 2 times as long, and the afterimage lasted almost 2 times as long.
maths.explain: 60 seconds is 2 lots of 30 seconds, so you stared 2 times as long. The afterimage lasted 15 seconds instead of 8. 8 + 8 = 16, and 15 is nearly 16. So it lasted almost twice as long. The longer the cones work, the more tired they get.
maths.context: This is about the Blue Mango. You stare at a blue mango drawing, then see a yellow mango on white paper, because some of your colour cells are tired.
maths.why_maths: Comparing 'how many times longer' shows whether two things grow together. Here, more staring means a longer ghost.
