roots.context: We have been learning how each sense detects the world and turns it into signals for the brain. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: With your nose pinched, elaichi sugar tastes only sweet. Let go, and the elaichi comes back. Your nose detected it, yet you felt it in your mouth. So your brain decides where each feeling seems to be.
deep_truth.habit: We think a feeling happens where we feel it, so flavour must be on the tongue. But the brain places every feeling, using all the signals it gets. Most of flavour comes from the nose, and the brain puts it in the mouth.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Hold Your Nose test, the spiced sugars tasted just sweet with the nose pinched. With the nose open, the spice came back, and it still seemed to be on the tongue. Scientists have found the same: smells from food in the mouth are felt as tastes.

three.who_am_i: The elaichi seemed to be on your tongue, but your nose found it. You do not sense with one part at a time. Your whole body and brain sense together.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing senses something. A bacterium senses sugar, a bee senses ultraviolet, and you sense a mango. Being alive means sensing the world and acting on what you sense.
three.what_is_this_world: The world holds far more than any animal can sense. Each creature detects only a small part of it, and builds its own world from that.

roots.thread: Your senses detect very different things: light, vibrations, pushes, warmth, gravity, the stretch of your muscles and many kinds of molecules. Yet every one of them becomes the same kind of electric signal. The brain joins all these signals into one world, so the mango you see, smell and taste is one mango. The same awareness is present in every creature that senses, from a bacterium to a bee to you. Each one senses its own part of the same world.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 35.23, the Sabba Sutta (the Buddha's teaching on 'the All')
teachings.teaching: The Buddha was asked, 'What is the All?' He named six pairs. The eye and what it sees. The ear and sounds. The nose and smells. The tongue and tastes. The body and touches. The mind and thoughts. That, he said, is the All.
teachings.link: This unit found the same pairs: a receptor and what it detects, like a cone and light, or a smell cell and a molecule. The Buddha also counted the mind as a sense. In this unit, the brain joined the signals from the nose and tongue into one flavour.

teachings.teaching: The body is like a chariot. The senses are the horses, and the things they sense are the roads. The mind is the reins, and understanding is the driver. The Self, the one who experiences, rides in the chariot.
teachings.link: Senses carry signals in from the world, like horses running along roads. The Upanishad asks who is riding. Science can follow the signals into the brain, but it cannot yet explain who or what experiences them.

teachings.teaching: The five colours can blind the eye. The five notes can deafen the ear. The five flavours can dull the tongue.
teachings.link: The Tao Te Ching warns that chasing strong colours, sounds and flavours dulls the senses. Science has found something related. In the Fading Coin activity, your skin stopped feeling a coin that did not move. A sense given the same thing for a long time stops reporting it.

science.text: Every sense works by receptor cells detecting something from the world and turning it into electric signals for the brain.
Nobody knows how electric signals in the brain become experiences, like the taste of mango. This is sometimes called the hard problem of consciousness.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, and many brain scientists today
other_view.view: The Charvaka thinkers taught that what the senses perceive is the only sure way of knowing, and that awareness ends when the body ends. Many brain scientists today agree in their own way: awareness is something the brain does, and there is no One behind it. These are honest views, held by thoughtful people.

practice.title: Circles of listening
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. First, listen for the furthest sound you can hear. Maybe a horn, or a bird far away. Now listen for something nearer, inside the house. how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle in ancient Greece, Charles Bell and Alexander Crum Brown in Scotland, Pierre Flourens in France, Ernst Mach and Josef Breuer in Austria, and Charles Sherrington in England
how_we_found_out.story: About 2,350 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle wrote a book called On the Soul. In it he listed five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Each one had a body part you could point to: eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin. Aristotle also argued that there could be no sixth sense. He was so respected that books copied his list for about 2,000 years. It was also easy to teach, because every sense had an organ to show. But some senses have no organ you can see. In the 1820s, a Scottish surgeon called Charles Bell described a 'muscle sense' that tells you where your arms and legs are. In 1906, Charles Sherrington named it proprioception. Also in the 1820s, a French scientist, Pierre Flourens, damaged the tiny curved tubes deep inside pigeons' ears, and the birds lost their balance. In 1873 and 1874, three scientists, Ernst Mach, Josef Breuer and Alexander Crum Brown, each worked out that these tubes sense the head turning. Today scientists count many senses, from about a dozen to over 30, and they do not agree on one number. Textbooks still say five because it is an old habit, not because it is true.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed there were exactly five senses, one for each organ you can see. Senses with no organ to point at, like the muscle sense and the balance sense of the inner ear, showed that the list was far too short.
